A Princess leader adds one attack. When a squad’s leader is a Princess who is still standing and not petrified, every other member of the squad gets one extra attack in the battle.

Every attack goes through the hit check and damage calculation; see Accuracy and evasion and Damage.

Who acts when

A battle is played out in steps. At each step, every character who still has an attack left takes part, and a character with more attacks keeps taking part after others have run out.

Within a step, characters act one row at a time. Each side starts with its front row and works back. The game compares the next row due on each side by a speed score, and the faster row acts first; if the scores are equal, your row goes first. Inside a row, the character with higher AGI goes first.

Row speed

Characters in the rowRow speed score
OneThat character’s AGI
TwoThe two AGIs added together
ThreeThe average of the two highest AGIs, plus the lowest

One event changes this order: when a wild monster turns down Talk, it strikes back at once. Its row goes first, and every attack it has already made in the battle is given back, so it can attack its full number of times again. Combined spells can also change the order.

Tactics

The squad’s tactic chooses which enemy each attack aims at, from the enemies that attack can reach.

TacticTargetAlignment term
AutonomousA random enemy−1
Attack StrongestThe enemy with the most current HP0
Attack LeaderThe enemy leader when it can be reached; otherwise a random enemy+1
Attack WeakestThe enemy a rough damage estimate rates highest0

“Attack Weakest” doesn’t look for the lowest HP. For each enemy it makes one damage estimate, including the usual random spread, and aims at the highest. It ignores hit chance and whether the enemy has less HP left than the estimate, so it usually picks the enemy with the weakest defense or resistance, not the easiest kill. The Alignment term shifts the Alignment change, up or down, when one of your characters defeats an enemy; see Alignment.

Action points

Each battle has up to three action points. A battle starts with none and the first arrives almost at once. After that, points fill from two sources: time, and damage your own squad takes. Training battles and a few special battles allow only two.

How action points fill

SourceHow much it fills
Time, holding one pointThe next point after about 600 frames, roughly 20 seconds
Time, holding two pointsThe next point after about 1,200 frames, roughly 40 seconds
Time, with battle animations turned offThe same amounts, 1.6 times faster
Damage your characters takeOne point for every 150 HP they lose, counting each loss only down to 0 HP

Times assume the battle updates once per frame at 30 frames a second.

So a squad that is taking heavy hits earns points much faster than one that isn’t.

What action points pay for

CommandCost
Change tactic1 (choosing the tactic you already have is free)
Talk (wild-monster battles only)1
The two-point command, which ends the battle at once as your loss2

A squad carrying a Charge Horn starts with three, or two in a battle capped at two; see Items. For Talk, see Wild monsters.

Who wins

When the battle ends, the game decides the result in this order:

SituationResult
A boss battle (see below) and the enemy leader is still standingYou lose
A boss battle and the enemy leader has fallen or been petrifiedYou win
Only your side has characters still able to fightYou win
Only the enemy side has characters still able to fightYou lose
Neither side has anyone able to fightDraw
Both sides still stand, and exactly one squad can’t move on the map (Immobile type)The squad that can’t move wins
Both sides still stand, and both squads are ImmobileDraw
Both sides still standThe side that received less damage wins; equal damage is a draw

A squad with a Vampire is Immobile during the day; otherwise only special story units are. Fallen and petrified characters don’t count as able to fight. Afterwards the two-point command always makes the battle a loss, a successful Talk a win, and some story events can force a loss.

Boss battles. When you fight a mission’s boss squad, damage doesn’t decide anything: you must defeat or petrify the enemy leader, or the battle counts as your loss. The same rule applies to any squad led by Danika in her boss form, and to a few second boss squads: Amrius’s first squad in Royal Blood (#31), Ruolanair or the first Knight of Danika in March on the Capital (#37), Procus in Promises (#38), Baldwin in The Sleeping Goddess (#42), and all five of Destin, Debonair, Gilbert, Aisha, and Saradin in Caliber (#43), depending on the route. Training battles and a few special battles never use it.

“Received” means the HP your own side actually lost, counting each character’s loss only down to 0. The result affects experience in training battles and some story battles; see Experience.

Tips

  • Put each class in its best row. An Archer shoots twice from the middle or back but once from the front; a Knight slashes twice from the front but once elsewhere.
  • Attack Leader focuses fire. Every attack that can reach the enemy leader goes to the leader.
  • Use Attack Weakest against tough defenses. It aims at the enemy it expects to hurt most, which usually means the one with the weakest defense or resistance.
  • Use Attack Leader against bosses. Against a boss squad only the enemy leader matters, so aim every attack at the leader.
  • Shield your casters. Most spellcasters attack twice only from the back row.

Battle glossary

Formation row

The front, middle, or back row of a squad’s formation. A character’s row decides which attack they use and how many times.

Tactic

The squad-wide targeting order: Autonomous, Attack Strongest, Attack Leader, or Attack Weakest.

Action points

Points that build up during a battle, usually up to three. Changing tactic costs one, Talk in a wild-monster battle costs one, and the two-point command ends the battle as a loss.

Modder reference: Battle turns, rows, and tactics

A battle runs in steps. At each step the scheduler gathers the actors who still owe an attack, orders them by side and row, the squad tactic chooses each target, and the damage chain resolves the hit. Row actions and counts are class data; the Princess bonus, tactics, and the result rules are code.

Where these facts come from

Locations and values were read from the US retail ROM (z64); the main combat overlay runs at z64 + 0x7FFBCD30. The result rules are the independently reviewed rules from the automatic-class-change research. None of the suggested edits has been tried in a running game yet, so test each one from a cold boot before relying on it.

Where the data lives

DataLocation (z64)FormatIn the Editor
Row actions and countsClass stats origin +43..+483 × [action ID, count]Classes tab (row attacks)
Action names0x00060988 + 16 × (id − 1) + 4RAM name pointerCombat actions
Tactic labels / Alignment terms0x0005CEC4 / 0x00239CD04 pointers / 4 signed bytes—

Class records are inside the CRC-checked region; the Editor fixes the checksum on export. Retail counts reach 3, or 4 with the Princess-leader bonus. Counts above 8 have run in combat; the known crash is the whole battle’s action stream overflowing 0x800 bytes, not any single count.

What do you want to change?

Give a class more attacks

Raise a row count. Retail stays at 1–3; high counts overflow the action stream without the Editor’s stream fix.

See Class row block · Step schedule

Change what a tactic targets

Needs a code change in the target selector.

See Tactic target selection

Change how fast action points build

Change the rate numerators (z64 0x00229A60, 0x00229A70, 0x00229A80) and, for the threshold, every copy of 260.0 together: 0x00229A98, the loop compare 0x00229AA8, the spend compares 0x00229978–0x00229988, the 259.0 start at 0x00215364, and the 260.0 pin at 0x0021B084.

See Action points

How to read the code and byte evidence

ROM offsets use big-endian z64 order. The master v64 stores each byte pair in reverse order. RAM addresses belong to the stated overlay or structure.

Each code line shows the z64 offset, the four original bytes, and the MIPS instruction. Relative branches name z64 destinations; J/JAL targets are encoded RAM addresses. The instruction after a branch is its delay slot.

Samples are stored bytes, not calculated values. For compressed resources, the sample gives the container’s ROM offset and the offset inside the decoded file.

Class row blockStep scheduleTactic target selectionAction pointsBattle result rules

Class row block

Each class stores one action and one count per row. Spell actions 45–47 and 145 (General’s own group) take their element from equipment, as the Unity tab explains; 51–54 have fixed elements (record byte +9: Lightning 01, Healing 05, Healing Plus 05, Nightmare 06).

Fighter 04 02 04 01 04 01; Amazon 0E 01 0E 01 0E 02; Wizard 2D 01 2D 01 2D 02.
Princess bonus
Actor setup func_0020DB10 (0x0020DFA8–0x0020E000, and 0x0020E8B8–0x0020E910 for the other side) and func_0020CB64 find the same-side leader (flag 0x200). If it is class 0x21, not dead or petrified, every other actor’s owed count +0x70 = row count + 1.

Class 0x4D row bytes are 00 FF 00 FF 00 FF, placeholder data.

Step schedule

The builder func_00231CC0 fills six 36-byte buckets (codes 0, 1, 2, 6, 7, 8; 6–8 folded onto 3–5), each up to three actors sorted by u16 +0x2C AGI descending. It scores buckets (1 actor: AGI; 2: sum; 3: mean of the top two + the lowest), takes each side’s front-most bucket still owed an attack (highest code among 0–2, lowest among 6–8), and puts the higher score first, player on a tie (0x00232074–0x00232184). The consumer func_00232D7C runs bucket 0 only, rebuilds, and advances the step (context +0) when nothing is left.

Actor fields
+0x2C AGI (battle copy), +0x58 position (enemy cell/3 = 0–2, player 8 − cell/3 = 6–8; set at 0x0020DF08–0x0020DF28 and 0x0020E804–0x0020E834), +0x6C attacks done, +0x70 attacks owed.
Row table
z64 0x0021311C = 02 01 00 FF FF FF 00 01 02 maps positions to rows, so 2 and 6 are front rows.
Forced first
func_00232280 runs only in random-neutral battles (func_0020BF6C) when owner byte +0x6074 is set. Talk (func_00219A14) sets it at 0x00219AA8 on result code 2 (“was not persuaded”), then re-plans the action stream through func_00232D7C (0x00219E44), which resets the step to 0 (0x00232DE0). The first living opponent actor’s bucket is moved to the front, keeping the others in order. If it is in no bucket, its +0x6C (attacks done) is decremented, the buckets rebuilt, and func_00232280 recurses (jal 0x801EEFB0, itself) until it is found, so every attack it has made is given back. The flag clears at 0x00232404.

Watch out for

  • Group checks 0x801ED7CC / 0x801EC2B0 can replace per-slot acting, probably for combined spells.

Tactic target selection

The squad tactic, read through 0x801CA384, picks one target from the candidate list the action allows. Attack Weakest calls func_00237750(att, tgt, 0, 0): flags 0 leave the ±10% random factor on (bit 0x2 at 0x00237550 clear), so each candidate gets one randomized roll. It ignores hit chance and isn’t capped at the target’s remaining HP.

Labels
Autonomous, Attack Strongest, Attack Leader, Attack Weakest.
Alignment
The same index selects the kill-adjustment term (−1, 0, +1, 0) described on the Alignment tab.

Action points

Points gate mid-battle commands. They start at 0 with the gauge at 259.0, one short of the 260 threshold, so the first arrives almost at once; the rate falls as points rise (260/30, 260/600, and 260/1200 per unit of elapsed time, plus a second a1·260/150 term). The normal cap is 3. When the training predicate (func_0020BF7C) or the preservation predicate (func_0020BF8C) is set, func_0021AE74 (0x0021B04C–0x0021B090) caps points at 2 and pins the gauge at 260.0, which also trims a Charge Horn’s 3.

Commands
Menu slot 0 in a random-neutral battle (func_0020BF6C at 0x00215F60) is Talk: −1 (0x00215FB4), then phase 6 (func_00219A14). Slot 1 needs ≥ 2 (0x0021609C), is prompted first when byte 0x801936E0 is set, subtracts 2 (0x00216168), and writes override 1, a loss (0x00216188). Tactic change −1 at 0x00216458; re-selecting the current tactic is free (beq at 0x00216424).
Phase table
func_0021B894 dispatches phase +0x6044 − 2 through z64 0x00229D80; phase 6 → func_00219A14.
Gauge update
func_0021AE74(t, a1): gauge +0x1AC += t × 260/30, 260/600, or 260/1200 (0, 1, or 2 points held; nothing at 3), then += a1 × 260/150; at ≥ 260 it subtracts 260 and adds a point. Time callers: func_0021B0A0 (0x0021B290–0x0021B2BC) passes t = 1.0 when byte 0x800E9C12 = 1 (combat body animation enabled), 1.6 otherwise, 0 when global 0x801CE8C4 is clear; func_00215CF0 passes 1.0 from the menu state, only while 0x801CE8C4 is clear, so the two time callers never add in the same frame. Byte 0x800E9C12 is written from options record 9, “Battle animation”. Damage callers: func_0021EBBC (0x0021FA48, 0x0021FC40, 0x0021FF54) pass a1 = HP lost, capped at remaining HP, with t = 0, only for player-side actors (func_0020C014, flag 0x100 clear).

Battle result rules

The result callback counts survivors (not dead, not petrified, not flag 0x1000) on each side. One-sided survival decides; both sides surviving goes to a unit-state test and then damage received; nobody surviving is a draw. Overrides apply last.

Order
Training and preservation battles skip the special checks. Then the special-opponent predicate, the survivor counts, the Immobile test, damage received, and finally the overrides.
Boss rule
func_00213B50 (live 0x801D0880) is true when the opponent squad’s leader class (char +0x11) is 0x87, when opponent source 0x801976E8 = 0x1E (the mission boss), when key 0x801936A7 = 0x3B and source 0x1E–0x22, or when source = 0x1F and key is 0x27, 0x2D–0x2F, 0x34, or 0x3C (table z64 0x002298D0). Then the opponent leader from func_0020C788 decides: alive and not petrified → result 1, otherwise 0 (0x00215528–0x00215568). Key 0x2D’s source 0x1F is Ruolanair (class 0xA2); key 0x2E’s is the first Knight of Danika; key 0x3B’s sources 0x1E–0x22 are Destin, Debonair, Gilbert, Aisha, and Saradin. Keys 0x35 and 0x36 load the same Baldwin row as 0x34 but aren’t in the table.
Immobile rule
The value-7 test reads squad-record byte +0x18 at 0x80197208 + 25 × id for 0x801976DC and 0x801976E8. That byte is the squad movement type written by func_0006D7D8 from the priority reducer, so 7 = Immobile. Other writers of the same byte include z64 0x0011A21C, 0x0011A300, 0x001A1EE8, 0x001AEF30, and 0x001B72DC.
Magnus check
At 0x002153E8–0x00215470 the callback requests combat phase 3 for training and preservation battles, and otherwise when the player leader (func_0020C810), with both class fields in 0x51–0x53 (Magnus), is dead or petrified. What phase 3 then does for Magnus hasn’t been followed.
Overrides
Flag 0x0400 in +0x606A forces a loss; +0x606A is refreshed through func_002224F4 (batch XP writeback, then resident event checks with trigger 0x10) after each death or petrification, so its bits come from story-event checks. Override 1 from the 2-point menu command (0x00216188) a loss; override 2 (0x0021A8B0, paired terminal owner) and 3 (Talk success, 0x00219D1C) a win.

COMBAT SYSTEMS

Status effects

What each ailment does, how long it lasts, and how to get rid of it.

Status effects either stop a character from attacking or change their attributes for the rest of the battle. Almost all of them end when the battle does. Petrification and death are the exceptions, and they stay with the character until you deal with them.

Effects at a glance

EffectIn battleLasts untilRemoved by
SleepCan’t attack; rolls to wake each time their turn to attack comes upThey wake, are cured, or the battle endsWaking up; combined Healing
ParalysisCan’t attack; rolls to recover each time their turn to attack comes upThey recover, are cured, or the battle endsRecovering; combined Healing
PetrificationCan’t actCured, even after the battle endsRevive Stone; Altar of Resurrection; combined Healing
PoisonSTR, VIT, INT, MEN, AGI, DEX, and Luck drop by 10%Cured, or the battle endsCombined Healing
Power UpThe same attributes rise by 10% per doseThe battle endsCancelled by Power Down
Power DownThe same attributes drop by 10% per doseThe battle endsCancelled by Power Up
DeathCan’t actRevived, even after the battle endsAltar of Resurrection

Combined Healing means Healing or Healing Plus cast by two or three casters as a combined spell. It is the only attack or spell that cures ailments. A single caster’s Healing restores HP but cures nothing. None of these effects runs on a timer.

Sleep and Paralysis

A sleeping or paralyzed character can’t attack. Each time their turn to attack comes up, they make a recovery roll instead, and that turn is used up whether or not they succeed.

Chance to recover = Luck + 1%
Luck 99 or higher always recovers
LuckChance each turn
01%
2526%
5051%
7576%
99 or moreAlways

The roll uses the character’s own Luck in battle, so Poison and Power Down make recovery harder. A poisoned character with Luck 50 drops to Luck 45 and a 46% chance. Luck bonuses from equipment don’t count.

Sleep has a second way out. A physical hit that doesn’t kill the sleeper gives them a chance to wake up, unless they are also paralyzed or petrified. A Sleep weapon such as Evil Blade or Brionac can put them straight back to sleep with the same blow. A character who is both asleep and paralyzed rolls against Paralysis first.

Disabled characters are easy targets because ordinary attacks can’t miss someone who is asleep, paralyzed, or petrified. They also can’t take part in combined spells or Soldier group attacks until they recover.

Petrification

A petrified character can’t act. Unlike the other ailments, Petrification stays after the battle ends. Outside battle you can cure it with a Revive Stone or at an Altar of Resurrection. During battle, only combined Healing removes it.

Petrification also shuts a character out of after-battle changes. They can’t evolve, and their Alignment goes back to its value at the start of the battle instead of moving toward the squad average.

Training battles, and some story battles, restore every character’s HP and status afterward, so Petrification from those battles doesn’t stick.

Gaze of Terror

Gaze of Terror skips the normal hit check. It petrifies its target unless the target carries a light or heavy shield in any equipment slot, or is immune to Petrification. A Golem that meets the Stone Golem requirements becomes a Stone Golem instead of turning to stone.

Poison, Power Up, and Power Down

These three effects don’t cost turns. They change STR, VIT, INT, MEN, AGI, DEX, and Luck for the rest of the battle, and that feeds into damage, defense, accuracy, evasion, and recovery rolls. HP, maximum HP, and level are unaffected.

  • Poison lowers each attribute by 10%. A second dose adds nothing.
  • Power Down lowers each attribute by 10% per dose, and doses stack.
  • Power Up raises each attribute by 10% per dose, and doses stack. One Power Up cancels one Power Down.

Every step is 10% of the character’s normal attributes, not of their current value, so the steps add up evenly instead of compounding:

Attribute in battle = Normal attribute × (1 + 0.1 × Power Ups − 0.1 × Power Downs − 0.1 if poisoned)
Normal attribute 200 with…Attribute in battle
Normal attribute200
Poison180
One Power Down180
Poison and one Power Down160
One Power Up220
Two Power Ups240
Poison and one Power Up200

Results are rounded down, and attributes stay between 0 and 999, with Luck between 0 and 100. Near a rounding boundary the game can land one point away from the formula. A 10% change in an attribute is not a 10% change in damage; see Damage for how attributes feed the calculation.

Combined Healing removes Poison and restores the lost 10% at once, but it leaves Power Up and Power Down in place. The only ways to clear a Power change are the opposite effect or the end of the battle.

One oddity is that when a Sleep, Paralysis, or Petrification weapon replaces Poison, the Poison is gone but its 10% penalty is not lifted straight away.

Death and undead

A character at 0 HP is dead. They can’t act, and they stay dead after the battle until you revive them at an Altar of Resurrection. Healing spells restore HP to the living but don’t revive the dead.

Undead characters recover on their own. When a scenario ends, every Zombie, Skeleton, and Ghost on your roster returns to full HP, including any that fell in battle.

Holy attacks destroy undead for good

If one of the attacks or weapons below deals a killing blow to a Zombie, Skeleton, or Ghost, that character is deleted from your army. Not even an Altar of Resurrection can bring them back. A holy hit that doesn’t kill does ordinary damage.

SourceNames
Spells and attacksBanish, Jihad, Magic Missile, Sacred Breath, Divine Ray, Ignis Fatuus
WeaponsBlessed Sword, Penitence, Oracion, Chaladholg, Kusanagi, Needle of Light, Anbicion, Clau Solace, Celestial Hammer, Rune Axe, Holy Lance, Lance of Longinus, Holy Comet, Vajra, Crescente, Ytival, Celestial Mace, Gambantein, Airgetlam, Heaven’s Doll, Lia Fail, Caldia

This matters most for your own undead, because an enemy’s holy attack removes them in the same way. Training battles and some story battles don’t remove anyone.

Immunity

Immunity protects against Sleep, Paralysis, Petrification, and Poison. It can come from a character’s class or from any item they have equipped, and one source is enough. Nothing gives immunity to Power Up, Power Down, or holy removal.

EquipmentProtects against
Hallowed ShieldSleep, Paralysis, Petrification, and Poison
Saint’s Shield; Elder’s SignParalysis
Purified Robe; Freude HelmSleep
Celestial VeilPetrification
ClassImmune to
Ghost; Stone Golem; Baldr GolemSleep, Paralysis, Petrification, and Poison
Lich; Vampire*; Zombie; Skeleton; GolemSleep, Paralysis, and Poison
Gorgon*Poison
Soldier; Cockatrice; Gladiator; Vanguard; GeneralPetrification

Every other standard class has no immunities. *Some classes exist in more than one version, and the versions don’t always match. One of the two Vampire versions has no immunities, and a second Gorgon version is immune to all four ailments. Many story bosses resist Sleep, Paralysis, and Petrification.

When ailments overlap

A character can’t have the same ailment twice, but different ailments can overlap. Whether a new ailment takes hold depends on how it is delivered. For this purpose the ailments rank from strongest to weakest as Petrification, Paralysis, Sleep, then Poison.

Delivered byWhat happens
A status spell, such as Slumber Mist or Poison CloudAdds its ailment on top of whatever the target already has.
An extra effect on a damaging attack, such as Sleep from MesmerizeFails if the target already has that ailment or a stronger one. Extra Poison won’t take hold on a sleeping target, and extra Sleep won’t take hold on a paralyzed one.
A weapon hitReplaces weaker ailments. A Sleep weapon removes Poison, a Paralysis weapon removes Sleep and Poison, and a Petrification weapon removes Sleep, Paralysis, and Poison.

Power Up and Power Down are not ailments, so they stack with everything and none of these rules apply to them.

What causes each effect

Status effects arrive in three ways, and each way has different odds.

  • Status spells use the same hit check as any other attack, then the target’s immunity.
  • **Extra effects** come with a damaging attack. The attack has to hit, and then a second roll must come in under half, or a quarter, of that attack’s hit threshold. With a hit threshold of 80, a half-threshold effect lands on 40% of hits.
  • Weapons apply their ailment on every hit that doesn’t kill, with no extra roll. Immunity still applies.
EffectStatus spellExtra effect: half the hit thresholdExtra effect: a quarter of the hit thresholdWeapon
SleepSlumber Mist, Nightmare, Deep Sleep, Black BreezeMesmerize, Abyss, Clear Disaster, Evil Dead, Atmosphere, InfernoIonosphere, InfestEvil Blade, Brionac
ParalysisShock Bolt, Ray of Paralysis, Bind Flare, Poison PlantRadiant Gale, Plasma Storm, Lava FlowPlasma Ball, Lava ShotDagda’s Hammer, Doll of Curse

AttackEffect
Earthquake; Gremlin’s Throw a KissPower Down whenever the attack hits

For how the hit threshold itself is calculated, see Accuracy and evasion.

Status effects and evolution

After-battle evolution checks a character’s attributes as they stand at the end of the battle, including any Power Up, Power Down, or Poison. A Power Up can therefore push a monster over an evolution requirement early, while Poison or Power Down can hold one back.

For example, a Young Dragon needs VIT 114, INT 73, and MEN 101 to become a Platinum Dragon, along with its Alignment requirement. A dragon with 110, 70, and 95 falls short, but one Power Up raises those to 121, 77, and 104, which is enough.

There is a catch. If the character levels up in that battle, the game reloads their normal attributes before the evolution check, so temporary changes no longer count.

Good to know

  • Names can mislead. Poison Plant paralyzes, Doom poisons, and Crimson Note causes Power Down.
  • Earthquake normally can’t hit flying characters, but it can hit a flying character who is asleep, paralyzed, or petrified.

Status glossary

Normal attributes

A character’s attributes as they stand outside battle, before Poison and Power changes. Every Poison and Power step is 10% of these values. Equipment bonuses are added separately.

Recovery roll

The roll a sleeping or paralyzed character makes each time their turn to attack comes up. The chance is Luck + 1%, and the turn is used up whether or not it succeeds.

Extra effect

An ailment carried by a damaging attack. The attack has to hit first, then a second roll decides whether the ailment takes hold.

Combined Healing

Healing or Healing Plus cast by two or three casters together as a combined spell. It cures Sleep, Paralysis, Petrification, and Poison, but leaves Power Up and Power Down in place. A single caster’s Healing restores HP and cures nothing.

Modder reference: Status Effects

Status effects come from four pieces of data. The attack table says what each attack inflicts. The class table and item byte B24 decide who is immune, and item byte B23 gives weapons an on-hit ailment. A few constants in code set how strong Poison and Power are, and everything else is battle-engine code.

Where these facts come from

Every location and value on this tab was read from the US retail ROM, and offsets are z64. None of the suggested edits has been tried in a running game yet, so test each one from a cold boot before relying on it.

Where the data lives

The attack and item tables sit inside the CRC-checked region (z64 0x1000–0x100FFF), so recalculate the CIC-6102 checksum after a hex edit. The Editor does this on export. The class table and the code constants are outside that region.

One ailment can use a different bit in each table. For example, Poison is 01 in the class table but 20 in B24. Other known bits are B23 01 (anti-dragon attack) and B24 01 (anti-dragon defense). In the class table, bit 10 lets a class transform at scenario end and bit 20 lets its identity be replaced (see Automatic class changes). Battle flag 20 has no known meaning.

Extra-effect conditions (D9)

D9The extra effect in D7 applies when…
2Always; there is no extra roll (friendly Throw a Kiss)
5The action succeeded (Earthquake, combined Healing)
4The action hit and a fresh 0–99 roll is below ⌊H ÷ 2⌋
11 (0B)The action hit and a fresh 0–99 roll is below ⌊H ÷ 4⌋
6The action’s amount is at least the target’s HP (holy removal)

H is the action’s hit threshold from the Accuracy article. D6 selects the extra-effect family. Every extra effect on this page uses family 08, and FF means no extra effect. Other families exist; Life Drain uses 0B, for example. D8 is FF in every status action.

What do you want to change?

Make an attack inflict a different ailment, or add one

Edit the status bytes in its attack record, then check that the targets you care about aren’t immune.

See Attack table: which effect an attack applies · Immunity: class table and item byte B24

Make Poison or Power stronger or weaker

Each strength is one constant in code. Change the constant, then check how the change affects evolution.

See Poison, Power Up, and Power Down arithmetic · Temporary attributes and evolution

Give a class or item immunity

Set the ailment’s bit in the class table or in the item’s B24. The two tables use different bits for Poison.

See Immunity: class table and item byte B24

Change how quickly characters wake up or recover

The chance is a Luck comparison in code, and no table or duration counter controls it.

See Sleep and Paralysis recovery

Stop holy attacks from deleting undead

Remove the extra effect from the spells, or clear the bit on the weapons.

See Holy removal of undead

Work out why an ailment didn’t take hold

Check immunity, then the overlap rules, then any special success rule on the action.

See Immunity: class table and item byte B24 · Battle flags: applying, combining, and curing · Gaze of Terror’s shield rule (D5 = 3)

How to read the code and byte evidence

ROM offsets use big-endian z64 order. The master v64 stores each byte pair in reverse order. RAM addresses belong to the stated overlay or structure.

Each code line shows the z64 offset, the four original bytes, and the MIPS instruction. Relative branches name z64 destinations; J/JAL targets are encoded RAM addresses. The instruction after a branch is its delay slot.

Samples are stored bytes, not calculated values. For compressed resources, the sample gives the container’s ROM offset and the offset inside the decoded file.

Attack table: which effect an attack appliesImmunity: class table and item byte B24Gaze of Terror’s shield rule (D5 = 3)Battle flags: applying, combining, and curingSleep and Paralysis recoveryPoison, Power Up, and Power Down arithmeticEnd of battle: what is cleared and what is savedTemporary attributes and evolutionHoly removal of undead

Attack table: which effect an attack applies

Each action has a 16-byte record, made of a 4-byte name pointer followed by 12 data bytes, D0–D11. Status effects come from two places in those bytes. D3 is the primary effect, applied when the action itself succeeds. D7 is an optional extra effect, gated by the condition in D9. D6 is the extra-effect family, which is 08 for all status extra effects.

Location
D0 is at 0x00060980 + 16 × action ID, and the name pointer is the 4 bytes before it. Action IDs run 1–158.
Status bytes
D3 primary effect · D5 success rule (3 = shield rule) · D6 extra-effect family (08 = status) · D7 extra effect · D9 condition
Values
Effect codes and D9 conditions are in the tables above. Ordinary damaging actions have D3 = 1.
Example
Mesmerize (21) at 0x00060AD0: 04 06 03 01 01 01 08 04 FF 04 00 00. It deals damage (D3 = 1) with an extra Sleep (D7 = 4) on a half-threshold roll (D9 = 4).
Example
Poison Cloud (75) at 0x00060E30: 03 03 01 0A 00 08 FF FF FF FF 00 00. It poisons directly (D3 = 0A) and has no extra effect.
In the Editor
Not exposed. Edit the ROM directly and fix the checksum.

How to change it

To give a damaging spell an extra ailment, write the effect code to D7 and the condition to D9, and set D6 to 08. For example, 08 0A FF 04 at D6–D9 adds Poison on a half-threshold roll.

To change what a direct status spell inflicts, change D3. Slumber Mist (83) would become a Poison spell with D3 = 0A.

Watch out for

  • Names repeat. Throw a Kiss is two records: 23 grants Power Up and 24 inflicts Power Down. Deep Sleep, Bind Flare, Poison Lime, and others have one record per target area. Edit by action ID, and change every variant you mean to change.
  • D0 selects the action’s damage family, and other bytes control targeting and animation. Change only the status bytes unless you are prepared to test the whole action.
  • The table is inside the CRC region, and a ROM with a stale checksum freezes at boot.

Immunity: class table and item byte B24

A character resists an ailment when their class byte or any of their four equipped items has that ailment’s bit set. The game checks both the main class and the secondary class that named characters use, so a special class version can carry its own immunities. Only the four ailments have bits, so nothing blocks Power Up, Power Down, or holy removal.

Class table
0x008ACB32 + (class ID − 1): 164 uncompressed bytes (resource key 0x3188AE). Soldier (1) is 08 at 0x008ACB32; Lich (38) is 07 at 0x008ACB57.
Class bits
01 Poison · 02 Sleep · 04 Paralysis · 08 Petrification
Item byte
B24 at 0x00062310 + 32 × item ID + 24. Hallowed Shield (152) is 2E, which covers all four; Purified Robe (201) is 02.
Item bits
20 Poison · 02 Sleep · 04 Paralysis · 08 Petrification. Bit 01 is anti-dragon defense, not an immunity.
In the Editor
The Items tab shows B24 as a raw byte, though its hint still says “semantics unknown”. The class table is not exposed.
Code
func_002379AC matches an effect to its immunity category; func_0021062C combines class and item bits for a character.

How to change it

To make a class immune, OR its bit into the class byte. For example, changing 0x008ACB32 from 08 to 0A makes Soldiers immune to Sleep as well as Petrification. To give an item immunity, OR the item bit into its B24, either in the Items tab or in the ROM.

Watch out for

  • Poison is 01 in the class table but 20 in item B24. Using the wrong bit either does nothing or sets an unrelated flag.
  • Some classes exist in several versions with different bytes. Vampire is 43 (no immunities) and 44 (Sleep, Paralysis, Poison), and Gorgon is 49 (Poison) and 157 (all four). Change the ID the unit actually uses.
  • The same class byte also holds the scenario-end death flags: 10 allows an Angel Knight or Zombie change and 20 allows identity replacement. Change only the low four bits for immunity.
  • Item B24 is inside the CRC region; the class table is not.

Gaze of Terror’s shield rule (D5 = 3)

An action whose D5 byte is 3 skips the normal hit check. It succeeds unless the target has an item of type Light Shield (0x0E) or Heavy Shield (0x0F) in any of its four equipment slots. The target’s Petrification immunity is still checked afterward. Gaze of Terror (25) is the only retail action with D5 = 3.

Location
D5 is at 0x00060980 + 16 × action ID + 5, which is 0x00060B15 for Gaze of Terror.
Example
Gaze of Terror (25): 04 00 04 03 00 03 FF FF FF FF 00 00. D3 = 3 (Petrification) and D5 = 3.
Code
func_0022D14C, z64 0x0022DCEC–0x0022DD44; shield test func_0020C3B4; item-type read func_000454c8.
In the Editor
Not exposed.

How to change it

Setting D5 = 3 on another action should give it the same shield rule.

Watch out for

  • The other D5 values in retail (00, 01, 02, 07, 08, 09) are not mapped. Don’t assume 00 means an ordinary hit check.
  • The rule replaces the whole action’s success, not just the ailment, so a damaging action with D5 = 3 would be expected to miss shield users entirely.

Battle flags: applying, combining, and curing

In battle, a character’s ailments are bits in a 32-bit flags word. Effect codes are not the same thing: they select an operation, and the table above shows how the two map. Whether a new ailment can join existing ones depends on how it arrives, and each route below uses a different rule.

Battle flags
Battle actor +0x40, u32, in RAM: 01 Death · 02 Petrification · 04 Sleep · 08 Paralysis · 10 Poison.
Status spells
The action’s D3 effect ORs its flag in, and existing ailments don’t block it.
Extra effects
Petrification is set after its eligibility checks. Paralysis is rejected if flags & 0x0A, Sleep if flags & 0x0E, and Poison if flags & 0x1E.
Weapon hits
Clear, then set: Petrification clears 0x1C, Paralysis clears 0x14, and Sleep clears 0x10.
Cure (effect 11)
Clears 0x3E and rebuilds attributes, but leaves the Power float at +0x44 alone.
Code
func_0022B06C handles extra effects and the cure, z64 0x0022B06C–0x0022B1F4.

How to change it

The extra-effect rejection masks are constants in func_0022B06C, and the evidence listing below includes them. Changing a mask changes which existing ailments block that effect. Direct status spells skip these checks, so the masks don’t affect them.

Watch out for

  • A weapon hit that clears Poison doesn’t rebuild attributes, so the Poison penalty lingers until the next rebuild.
  • Death clears the ailment bits but keeps the Power float.
  • The cure mask includes bit 0x20, but nothing known sets it.

Sleep and Paralysis recovery

When a sleeping or paralyzed character’s action comes up, the game runs a recovery action instead. It clears the ailment when PRNG() % 100 is less than or equal to the character’s battle Luck. The action is spent either way, and there is no duration counter.

Luck used
Battle actor +0x30 (u8): Luck after Poison and Power, without equipment Luck.
Order
Paralysis is tested before Sleep when both are set.
Wake on hit
A successful nonlethal physical hit on a sleeper who isn’t also paralyzed or petrified triggers a wake-up check. The check runs before the weapon’s own ailment is applied.
Code
Sleep func_0022EDD4 (z64 0x0022EDD4–0x0022EE4C); Paralysis func_0022EC08; wake on hit func_0022A964.

How to change it

The chance comes from the comparison in each recovery function, not from a table, so any change is a code patch. Patch Sleep and Paralysis separately, and keep the action consumption intact.

Watch out for

  • Wake on hit is a separate path from the recovery action, so patch both if you want Sleep to behave consistently.
  • The wake-on-hit chance itself isn’t documented yet.

Poison, Power Up, and Power Down arithmetic

Power Up and Power Down add ±0.1 to a float accumulator at battle actor +0x44. Every change rebuilds all seven attributes from the character’s saved values: result = trunc(base + base × m), where m is the accumulator, minus 0.1 while poisoned. The result is narrowed to signed 16 bits, then clamped to 0–999, or 0–100 for Luck.

Power step
Built in each wrapper’s first two instructions. Power Up is lui a1,0x3DCC / ori a1,0xCCCD at 0x0021D784. Power Down is lui a1,0xBDCC / ori a1,0xCCCD at 0x0021D7A8.
Poison amount
IEEE double 3FB999999999999A (0.1) at 0x00229EF8, subtracted from the accumulator while poisoned.
Saved values
Read from the character record: player stride 56, deployed stride 52. Attributes are at +0x1C–+0x26 (six s16), and Luck is at +0x28.
Battle values
Actor +0x24–+0x2E (six s16) and Luck +0x30 (u8).
Code
Rebuild func_0021D450; wrappers func_0021D784 (Power Up), func_0021D7A8 (Power Down), and func_0021D7CC (rebuild only).

How to change it

To make Power Up worth 20%, change the halfword at 0x0021D786 from 3DCC to 3E4C, which makes the float 0x3E4CCCCD = 0.2. For Power Down, change 0x0021D7AA from BDCC to BE4C.

To make Poison take 20%, change the double at 0x00229EF8 to 3FC999999999999A.

Watch out for

  • Before changing the double at 0x00229EF8, check that nothing else loads it. This reference traces only its use by Poison.
  • Narrowing to signed 16 bits happens before the clamp. A large step can wrap a high attribute negative, and the clamp then sets it to 0 instead of 999.
  • Evolution reads these battle values (see Temporary attributes and evolution), so a stronger Power Up also makes early evolution easier.

End of battle: what is cleared and what is saved

At the end of battle, func_0021C140 builds clean values for the saved record. It resets the Power float, clears Sleep, Paralysis, and Poison (0x1C), and rebuilds the attributes before writing. Petrification is the only ailment that carries over. It is copied from battle flag 0x02 to the character’s saved status byte.

Saved status
Character record +0x33, bit 0x04 = petrified. This is the in-RAM player record, stride 56.
Cleared by
Revive Stone and Altar of Resurrection clear +0x33 & 0x04.
Preserved battles
Training and event-preservation battles restore the saved HP and status instead.
Code
func_0021C140 (z64 0x0021C140–0x0021C1BC); level-up caller func_00219470; attribute reload func_0021C074.

How to change it

To petrify or un-petrify a character in live RAM, set or clear bit 0x04 of +0x33 in their character record. To make another ailment persist after battle, you would need a new saved bit and a change to this export.

Watch out for

  • The battle bit (0x02) and the saved bit (0x04) differ.
  • The same function also restores a battle snapshot, so values seen partway through it are not the final state.

Temporary attributes and evolution

The evolution selector compares each character’s current battle STR–DEX, including Power and Poison, with the evolution row minima. It does not check level. When a character levels up in the results, the game exports them, applies the permanent level-up, and reloads battle attributes from the saved record without reapplying Power. After a level-up, only saved attributes count.

Selector
func_00219730 compares battle attributes with the evolution rows (see the Automatic Class Changes reference).
Level-up branch
z64 0x00219648–0x00219688 in func_00219470: export, level up, then reload.
Reload
func_0021C074 copies saved attributes and level but doesn’t reapply the Power float.

How to change it

To make evolution ignore temporary changes, point the selector at saved attributes or rebuild before the check. To let boosts count after a level-up, reapply the Power float after the reload. Both are code patches.

Watch out for

  • Test one battle with a level-up and one without, because they reach the selector with different attribute values.

Holy removal of undead

Holy removal is an extra effect, not an ailment. An action with D7 = 7 and D9 = 6 fires when its amount is at least the target’s HP and the target’s secondary class is 45–48 (both Zombie versions, Skeleton, and Ghost). Weapons do the same through item B23 bit 0x10 on an eligible killing hit. The result schedules battle events 0x30 and 0x31. In normal battles, event 0x31 deletes the character from the roster and unit.

Spells
Banish (28), Jihad (29), Magic Missile (30), Sacred Breath (36), Divine Ray (43), and Ignis Fatuus (154–156) all have D6–D9 = 08 07 FF 06.
Weapons
B23 bit 0x10 at 0x00062310 + 32 × item ID + 23. For example, Blessed Sword (15) has 10.
Removal
Event 0x31 reaches func_0021EBBC (z64 0x00220278–0x00220298 and 0x00220340–0x002203C4), which calls func_0004196C. The saved primary class becomes 0, which marks the roster slot empty.
Exempt
Training battles and event-preservation battles.
In the Editor
The Items tab shows B23 as a raw byte, though its hint still says “semantics unknown”.

How to change it

To stop a spell from deleting undead, set its D6 and D7 to FF. To stop a weapon, clear bit 0x10 in its B23. Protecting undead everywhere would need a patch to the eligibility check or to the event 0x31 branch.

Watch out for

  • Don’t make the condition unconditional. D9 = 6 is what limits removal to killing blows.
  • Removal empties the roster slot outright, so test on a copy of your save.

CHARACTER & CAMPAIGN

Alignment

What moves a character between Lawful and Chaotic, and what that changes.

Alignment is each character’s place on a scale from 0 (Chaotic) to 100 (Lawful). It decides which classes a character can change into and adjusts Virtue and Bane attacks. Averaged across a squad, it decides how liberated towns react. It changes mostly through kills and after-battle settling.

What Alignment affects

WhereWhat Alignment does
Class changesMany classes accept only characters within an Alignment range, and some automatic changes check it too.
Virtue and Bane attacksAdjusts attack power, defense, and resistance.
Liberating strongholdsThe squad’s average, compared with the town’s Morale, moves your Chaos Frame.
Menus and speechSorts the roster and chooses some leader lines, shop chatter, and scene text.
Lestat’s questionnaireThe visiting leader needs Alignment 0–49 to take part.

Three values are easy to mix up. A character’s Alignment belongs to that character alone. The squad average is worked out when it’s needed. Chaos Frame is a separate reputation for your whole army. Towns respond best to a squad that matches them, not to the most Lawful squad you can field.

A class’s starting Alignment only sets a new character’s first value. Changing class doesn’t reset it, and gaining levels doesn’t move it.

How Alignment changes

CauseChange
Scroll of Discipline+1, +2, or +3
Urn of Chaos−1, −2, or −3
Defeating an enemyFrom −5 to +5, depending on Alignment, level, and tactic (see below)
Each battle’s endUp to 3 points toward the average of your characters who fought
A new characterStarts at their class’s starting value; a few starting-roster characters are set to 50

Alignment never goes below 0 or above 100, so near either end you get less than the full change. A Scroll used at 99 always lands on 100, and the game won’t let you use a Scroll at 100 or an Urn at 0.

Recruited characters keep the Alignment they already had. Levelling up, changing class, and equipment leave it alone. No change from simply waiting or marching has been found. The Goblet of Destiny raises Luck, not Alignment.

Kills and after-battle settling

Attack Leader+1
Attack Weakest0

Add the three parts, keep the total between −5 and +5, and add it to the killer’s Alignment. For example, a killer at Alignment 60 defeats an enemy at 40 of the same level under Attack Leader. The difference of 20 gives +2, equal levels give 0, and Attack Leader adds +1, so the killer rises to 63.

In short, defeating more Chaotic enemies makes you more Lawful, and defeating weaker enemies makes you more Chaotic. That’s why a high-level character picking off weak foes can drift Chaotic even while fighting Chaotic enemies.

Some kills don’t count. Soldiers never gain or lose Alignment from kills, and killing a Soldier changes nothing. Enemy kills don’t change anyone’s Alignment. Gladiator Magnus, Warrior Dio, and Lord Destin are unaffected by their kills. When a combined attack defeats an enemy, more than one participant can be credited.

After the battle

When a battle ends, the game takes the average Alignment of your characters who fought. Soldiers are left out, but fallen characters count. Every surviving character, including Magnus, Dio, and Destin, then moves toward that average.

Average minus the character’s AlignmentChange
−100 to −51−3
−50 to −21−2
−20 to −6−1
−5 to 50
6 to 20+1
21 to 50+2
51 to 100+3

For example, two characters at 30 and 70 average 50, so they finish at 31 and 69. The average is fixed before anyone moves, and the kill changes are applied first.

Petrified characters count toward the average but don’t move. Instead, their Alignment returns to its value from the start of the battle, which also cancels any kill changes. Training battles change nothing, and some story scenes also leave Alignment alone.

Class requirements

Many classes accept only characters within an Alignment range. Both ends of the range count, so Paladin’s 60–100 accepts 60 and rejects 59. Alignment is only one requirement, and the class’s other requirements still apply.

ClassAlignment range
Knight40–100
Phalanx20–80
Paladin60–100
Black Knight0–40
Archmage0–40
Princess70–100
Angel Knight50–100
Seraph75–100

Automatic class changes can check Alignment too. A fallen character needs 50–100 to become an Angel Knight after a scenario, on top of other conditions and a random roll. See Automatic class changes.

Virtue and Bane attacks

Virtue and Bane attacks read Alignment three times. They use the attacker’s for power and the target’s for defense, then the target’s again for resistance. Every point away from 50 is worth a tenth of a point.

Virtue adjustment = (Alignment − 50) ÷ 10
Bane adjustment = (50 − Alignment) ÷ 10
AlignmentVirtueBane
0−5+5
30−2+2
5000
70+2−2
100+5−5

For power and defense, the adjustment is added to the percentage bonuses in the condition multiplier. At Alignment 70, a Virtue attacker’s power is multiplied by 1.02, not raised by 2 damage. The same adjustment is added to the target’s resistance against that element. See Damage for where each step fits.

A Lawful character therefore hits harder with Virtue and resists it better, and the reverse holds for Bane. Healing is a Virtue spell, but it skips resistance. A Lawful healer heals a little more, and a Lawful patient receives a little less, because their higher magic defense takes more off.

Alignment has no effect on ordinary hit chances.

Strongholds and Chaos Frame

When a squad liberates a stronghold, the game compares the squad’s average Alignment with the town’s Morale. The closer they are, the better the result for your Chaos Frame. The members’ own Alignment doesn’t change.

Score = difference between squad average and town Morale
+ town penalty (0 or 40)
+ random 0–7
ScoreChaos Frame
0–5+2
6–15+1
16–300
31–50−1
51–80−2
81–110−3
111–140−4
141 or more−5

The average covers every member of the squad at their current Alignment, not just the leader. Chaos Frame stays between 0 and 100. Some towns carry a 40-point penalty, and some skip this calculation and leave Chaos Frame alone. Whether a town is currently friendly or hostile doesn’t tell you which.

  • A squad averaging 50 at a town with Morale 50 scores 0–7, for +1 or +2 Chaos Frame.
  • A squad averaging 50 at a town with Morale 90 scores 40–47, for −1 Chaos Frame.
  • A squad averaging 50 at a town with Morale 50 and the 40-point penalty scores 40–47, for −1 Chaos Frame.

Match the squad to the town; Chaos Frame lists every town’s Morale. A very Lawful squad that liberates a low-Morale town can cost you Chaos Frame, which in turn changes your scenario Goth reward.

Menus, speech, and events

You can sort the roster by Alignment. Alignment also chooses some of what leaders say, including their shop commentary and neutral-encounter lines, and some scene text. These use three bands, and specific story classes override them.

Used forLowMiddleHigh
Leader lines and shop commentary0–3435–6566–100
Scene text0–3233–6566–100

Shop commentary is only flavour. Alignment doesn’t change prices or stock.

Lestat’s Bloody Emblem questionnaire

Lestat’s questionnaire needs the visiting squad’s leader to have Alignment 0–49. At 50 or above, it’s skipped. The event also checks the leader’s class and character type, whether you already hold a Bloody Emblem, and how far the event has progressed. Low Alignment lets you attempt it but doesn’t guarantee success.

Succeeding can award a Bloody Emblem, so make room in your inventory first. The event is marked complete before the game checks for space, so a full inventory costs you the item. The event doesn’t turn the leader into a Vampire by itself.

Talking to neutral monsters

Whether Talk succeeds in a neutral encounter doesn’t depend on Alignment. It depends on classes and HP, and Alignment only changes what the leader says.

Alignment glossary

Alignment

A character’s position on the scale from 0 (Chaotic) to 100 (Lawful). Each character has their own value, which moves with kills, after-battle settling, and two items.

Squad average Alignment

The members’ Alignment values added together and divided by how many there are, with any fraction dropped. Stronghold liberation uses every member of the squad. After-battle settling uses everyone who fought, except Soldiers.

Chaos Frame

Your army’s reputation, from 0 to 100. Liberating strongholds moves it up or down depending on how well each squad suits the town. It is separate from any character’s Alignment.

Town Morale

A stronghold’s own value that the liberating squad’s average Alignment is compared with. The closer the two are, the better the result for your Chaos Frame.

Killer

The character credited with the blow that brings an enemy to 0 HP. Only the killer’s Alignment moves from that kill.

Modder reference: Alignment

Alignment is one byte per character, and several things write to it. At battle start it is copied into the battle actor. During battle the kill rule changes that copy, after battle the settling rule changes it again, and then it is copied back. The kill and settling amounts come from small signed tables in ROM. Chaos Frame is a separate byte that only stronghold liberation writes.

Where these facts come from

Every location and value on this tab was read from the US retail ROM, and offsets are z64. None of the suggested edits has been tried in a running game yet, so test each one from a cold boot before relying on it.

Where the data lives

DataLocationFormatIn the Editor

Battle AlignmentBattle actor +0x34 (current) and +0x3F (start of battle)u8—

Kill table: Alignmentz64 0x00239CA011 signed (threshold, step) pairsNot exposed
Kill table: levelz64 0x00239CB811 signed (threshold, step) pairsNot exposed

The class starting Alignment at 0x0005DB38 is inside the CRC-checked region (z64 0x1000–0x100FFF); the combat tables and constants are outside it.

How the threshold tables read

TableRule
Kill: AlignmentScan pairs in order and use the step of the first pair whose threshold the difference (killer − enemy) meets. 4C 05 means a difference of 76 or more gives +5.
Kill: levelThe same, with each threshold read as a maximum. CD 05 means a difference of −51 or less gives +5.
Kill: tacticOne byte per tactic, in the order Autonomous, Attack Strongest, Attack Leader, Attack Weakest: FF 00 01 00.
Kill totalThe sum of the three parts, clamped to −5…+5, then the result clamped to 0…100
SettlingPairs in descending order; 33 03 means (average − current) of 51 or more gives +3.

These are ordered threshold lists, not arrays indexed by the difference. Keep each list sorted the way the original is.

What do you want to change?

Change how much a kill moves Alignment

Edit the kill tables. The tactic table is the simplest place to start.

See Kill change tables

Change after-battle settling

Edit the settling table’s steps, or its thresholds to widen or narrow the dead zone.

See After-battle settling table

Read or set a character’s Alignment

Use byte +0x1B of the character record, or the Save Game Editor.

See The character’s Alignment byte · How the save stores Alignment · Alignment during battle

Change a class’s starting Alignment or its requirements

Both are editable in the Classes tab.

See Class starting Alignment

Change Alignment’s effect on Virtue and Bane

Power and defense use one shared 0.1 factor, and resistance is handled separately in the damage routine.

See Virtue and Bane: attacker power · Virtue and Bane: target defense · Virtue and Bane: resistance, and Healing’s bypass

Change how towns react to a squad

The liberation rule compares the squad average with town morale and writes Chaos Frame.

See Stronghold liberation and Chaos Frame

How to read the code and byte evidence

ROM offsets use big-endian z64 order. The master v64 stores each byte pair in reverse order. RAM addresses belong to the stated overlay or structure.

Each code line shows the z64 offset, the four original bytes, and the MIPS instruction. Relative branches name z64 destinations; J/JAL targets are encoded RAM addresses. The instruction after a branch is its delay slot.

Samples are stored bytes, not calculated values. For compressed resources, the sample gives the container’s ROM offset and the offset inside the decoded file.

The character’s Alignment byte

Each character’s current Alignment is byte +0x1B of their 56-byte character record. The getter multiplies the character index by 56 and reads that byte. It is independent of Luck, the class starting value, and Chaos Frame.

Location
Character record +0x1B (u8), in the in-RAM roster of 100 records × 56 bytes.
Values
0–100 in normal play; 0 is valid (fully Chaotic).
Code
Getter func_00046358.
In the Editor
Save Game Editor, Alignment.

How to change it

To set a character’s Alignment, use the Save Game Editor or write the byte in live RAM outside battle. During battle, the battle actor’s copy is what counts (see Alignment during battle).

Watch out for

  • This is a RAM offset, not a save-file offset; the save packs fields (see How the save stores Alignment).
  • Persistent +0x34 is character identity, not Alignment. Only the battle actor stores Alignment at +0x34.

How the save stores Alignment

The save packs roster fields bit by bit, using a descriptor table. Alignment’s descriptor is 1B 01 07, meaning character offset 0x1B, one destination byte, and 7 packed bits.

Descriptor
z64 0x0005CF70: 1B 01 07.
Roster descriptor
z64 0x0005D344: 80 19 3B C0 00 00 00 38 80 18 70 34. The 38 is the 56-byte stride.
Range
7 bits can hold 0–127; the game uses 0–100.
In the Editor
The Save Game Editor unpacks and repacks this format and recomputes checksums.

How to change it

Edit saves through the Save Game Editor rather than by hand.

Watch out for

  • Values 101–127 fit in the save but are outside anything the game produces. Their effect isn’t known.

Alignment during battle

At battle start, func_0020D870 copies the character’s Alignment into two battle actor bytes. +0x34 is the live value that kills and settling change. +0x3F is a snapshot of the starting value, used to restore petrified survivors.

Fields
Battle actor +0x34 current (u8) · +0x3F start of battle (u8)
Code
func_0020D870, copy at z64 0x0020D908–0x0020D92C.

How to change it

To test Virtue/Bane or kill effects mid-battle, change +0x34. Changing only +0x3F affects what petrified survivors are restored to.

Watch out for

  • Actor and character records use different layouts, so check which structure a pointer refers to before using an offset.

Kill change tables

func_00233210 computes the kill change from three tables. It adds the Alignment part, the level part, and the tactic part, clamps the sum to −5…+5, adds it to the killer’s battle Alignment, and clamps the result to 0…100.

Alignment table
z64 0x00239CA0: 4C 05 33 04 1A 03 06 02 01 01 00 00 FB FF E7 FE CE FD B5 FC 9C FB (≥76 → +5 … ≥−100 → −5).
Level table
z64 0x00239CB8: CD 05 E6 04 F5 03 FC 02 FF 01 00 00 02 FF 09 FE 18 FD 31 FC 64 FB (≤−51 → +5 … ≤100 → −5).
Tactic table
z64 0x00239CD0: FF 00 01 00.
Excluded
Training, scripted preservation, Soldiers as killer or victim, enemy-side killers, and three named characters (Magnus, Dio, Destin).
Code
func_00233210, table walk at z64 0x002332D8–0x00233308.

How to change it

To make Attack Leader give +2, change the third tactic byte at 0x00239CD2 from 01 to 02. To reward killing Chaotic enemies more, raise the positive steps in the Alignment table, keeping the thresholds in order.

Watch out for

  • The −5…+5 clamp on the total is in code, so bigger table steps are cut off unless you change the clamp too.
  • The Alignment and level tables compare in opposite directions. Copy the pattern of the table you’re editing.

After-battle settling table

func_002333B4 computes one average for the battle’s player-side participants, leaving out Soldiers but keeping fallen characters. It then moves each eligible survivor toward that average by a step read from a seven-pair table. The average isn’t recomputed as people move.

Table
z64 0x00239CD4: 33 03 15 02 06 01 FB 00 EC FF CE FE 9C FD (≥51 → +3, ≥21 → +2, ≥6 → +1, ≥−5 → 0, ≥−20 → −1, ≥−50 → −2, ≥−100 → −3).
Receivers
Living, non-petrified, non-Soldier player characters. Petrified survivors are restored from +0x3F instead.
Code
func_002333B4, table walk at z64 0x002334E0–0x0023352C.

How to change it

To remove settling, set every step byte (the second of each pair) to 00. To make it stronger, raise the steps. To widen the dead zone, change the 06 and FB thresholds.

Watch out for

  • Recomputing the average after each move would be a different rule; the retail code fixes it first.

Class starting Alignment

When a character is created, func_0004501C reads their class’s starting Alignment and writes it to +0x1B. It is used once, at creation, and nothing resets a character to it later.

Location
z64 0x0005DB38 + 72 × class ID (u8). Fighter (2) is 32 = 50 at 0x0005DBC8.
Record origins
This byte is at +0x24 from the class record’s name/header origin (0x0005DB14) and +0x18 from its stats origin (0x0005DB20).
In the RAM copy
0x80187C38 + 72 × class ID.
In the Editor
Classes tab, Alignment. The Editor fixes the CRC on export.

How to change it

Use the Classes tab. By hand, change the byte and recalculate the checksum.

Watch out for

  • Pick one record origin and use its offsets throughout; mixing the name origin with stats-origin offsets lands on the wrong byte.
  • Class Alignment requirements are a separate table (stat-gate rows, bytes 6 and 7), also in the Classes tab.

Virtue and Bane: attacker power

When an attack’s element is Virtue, func_002351D4 adds (caster Alignment − 50) × 0.1 to the attack’s condition percentage. When the element is Bane, it adds (50 − Alignment) × 0.1. The 0.1 is a double constant in ROM.

Factor
z64 0x0023A0F0: 3F B9 99 99 99 99 99 9A (0.1).

Virtue and Bane: target defense

Defense conditions use the attacking action’s element and the target’s battle Alignment, with the same rule as power. This changes the target’s defense before resistance is applied. Healing uses it too, so a Lawful patient’s higher magic defense reduces the healing they receive.

Virtue and Bane: resistance, and Healing’s bypass

The damage routine builds final resistance from class, equipment, and the target’s Alignment term, then clamps it to 0–100. When kernel flag bit 0 is set, the finished resistance is forced to 0. Standard Healing (actions 87–90) sets that flag.

Resistance term
Virtue: + (target Alignment − 50) ÷ 10; Bane: + (50 − target Alignment) ÷ 10.
Code
func_0023697C (damage kernel), anchors at z64 0x002371AC–0x002373DC.

Stronghold liberation and Chaos Frame

func_0012FBB8 scores the squad’s average Alignment against the town’s morale. The score is |average − morale| plus 40 if the town’s morale byte has its high bit set, plus a random 0–7. The score picks a Chaos Frame change from +2 down to −5. Towns whose morale byte is FF skip the calculation.

Output
Chaos Frame at RAM 0x801936A9 (u8), kept within 0–100.
Bands
0–5 → +2 · 6–15 → +1 · 16–30 → 0 · 31–50 → −1 · 51–80 → −2 · 81–110 → −3 · 111–140 → −4 · 141+ → −5
Code
func_0012FBB8, write at z64 0x0012FDA8–0x0012FDD4.
Town data
Morale comes from the town’s ktenmain record, which the Editor’s Scenario tab edits. The Scenario rewards reference gives its layout.

How to change it

To make a town neutral to Alignment, give it morale FF so the calculation is skipped. Note that FF also has other meanings for towns (see Scenario rewards).

Watch out for

  • This writes only Chaos Frame; members’ Alignment is untouched.
  • The Editor keeps the morale byte’s high bit (the penalty) but doesn’t label it yet. A squad with no countable members is treated as averaging 50, and only player member IDs 1–98 count.

CHARACTER & CAMPAIGN

Automatic class changes

When monsters evolve, Soldiers graduate, and fallen characters rise as Angel Knights or Zombies.

Some class changes happen without your choosing them. Dragons and some beasts evolve after battle once their attributes are high enough, and Golems and undead change when struck by particular attacks. Soldiers graduate into Fighters or Amazons, and when a scenario ends, fallen characters can come back as Angel Knights or Zombies.

When class changes happen

WhenWhat can change
At the end of a battleDragons, some beasts, and Angel Knights can evolve. Soldiers can graduate.
When hit by certain attacksGolems, Zombies, and Skeletons
When a scenario endsFallen characters can become Angel Knights or Zombies.

This article covers only these automatic changes. Changing class from the menu, and class-changing items, work differently.

After-battle evolution

At the end of every battle, the game checks each of your characters against the evolution tables below. A character who meets every requirement in a row changes class. There’s no random roll, and they don’t need to have gained a level.

Each row checks the character’s class, their attributes at the end of the battle, their Alignment, and sometimes their Element. Element here means the character’s own Wind, Flame, Earth, or Water affinity, and no spellbook is needed. Minimums are inclusive, and so are Alignment ranges, so 25–75 accepts both 25 and 75.

Because attributes are read as they stand when the battle ends, Power Up can help a monster qualify and Poison or Power Down can hold it back. The exception is a character who also levelled up in that battle, whose normal attributes are used. See Status effects.

Fallen or petrified characters, Soldiers, and enemies don’t evolve, and nothing evolves after a training battle. A character evolves at most once per battle, even if they already meet the next class’s requirements.

Evolving keeps HP, maximum HP, attributes, level, Luck, and Alignment exactly as they were, so it doesn’t heal. For the rest of that battle the character may still appear in their old equipment. Afterwards, any slot left on the class default switches to the new class’s default, while items you chose yourself stay equipped.

When a Young Dragon qualifies for more than one

The game checks the rows in order: Platinum Dragon, then Black Dragon, then the four elemental dragons. The first row that passes wins. This matters where the ranges overlap. At Alignment 70–75, a dragon that meets Platinum Dragon’s attributes becomes a Platinum Dragon whatever its Element. At 25–30, Black Dragon likewise wins over the elemental dragons.

Angel Knight to Seraph

FromToMinimum attributesAlignmentElement
Angel KnightSeraphIntelligence 108, Mentality 125, Dexterity 12175–100Any

Seraph also needs a Needle of Light, Baldr Mail, and a Kite Shield, and you must own all three. Each one counts if it’s part of an Angel Knight’s default equipment, if the character is already wearing it, or if you have a spare that nobody is wearing.

An ordinary Angel Knight’s defaults already include the Needle of Light and Kite Shield, so in practice you need a spare Baldr Mail unless the Angel Knight already wears one. The check doesn’t use the item up. Once the battle is over, a Seraph still on default armour switches to Baldr Mail, but armour you chose yourself stays on.

Becoming an Angel Knight after a scenario follows a stricter rule, described under Changes after a scenario.

Soldier graduation

After a battle, a Soldier in your squad can be replaced by a brand-new Fighter or Amazon. This is called graduation. The new character is generated fresh and doesn’t inherit the Soldier’s level or attributes.

Earning progress

Graduation progress belongs to the squad’s leader. Each qualifying battle adds 2 points for every Soldier still standing, and a Medal of Vigor carried by the squad doubles that. In ordinary battles, a result qualifies when only your side can still fight, or when both sides are still standing but yours took less damage. Special battle rules can change this.

Each Soldier slot holds three soldiers who share one HP bar, and the game works out how many are still standing from that bar.

  1. Divide the slot’s maximum HP by 3, dropping any fraction. That is one soldier’s share.
  2. Divide the slot’s current HP by that share, rounding up, to a maximum of 3.
  3. Add up the standing soldiers from every qualifying slot, and multiply by 2, or by 4 with a Medal of Vigor.

For example, three standing soldiers give 6 points, or 12 with the Medal.

Graduating

At the end of any battle where the leader has 100 or more points, the game tries to create a graduate. You need room on your roster, which means fewer than 94 characters, and a spare set of starter equipment. If anything is missing, progress drops to 99, so the next qualifying battle tries again. A successful graduation resets it to 0. Training battles and neutral encounters never produce graduates, and some formations and story events block them too.

A Fighter leader produces a Fighter and an Amazon leader produces an Amazon. An Ansate Cross carried by the squad swaps the two.

GraduateSpare starter equipment needed
FighterShort Sword, Chain Mail, Round Shield, Iron Helm
AmazonShort Bow, Leather Armor, Bandanna

The graduate equips those spares, so you don’t lose any items.

The graduate’s attributes

The graduate starts at the level the scenario sets for new Soldiers, not the old Soldier’s level. They get a generated name, full HP, Luck 50, Alignment 50, and a random Element. Experience, fatigue, status, and graduation progress start at zero, and they use their class’s default equipment.

Attributes start at the level-1 base and grow for each level above 1. Each level adds the class’s growth plus two separate random 0-or-1 bonuses, so a Fighter gains 3–5 Strength per level. No attribute goes above 999.

Changes caused by attacks

Four changes happen in the middle of a battle, when the right attack strikes the right monster. There’s no level or Alignment requirement and no separate roll. The attack still has to succeed, though, and it has to leave the target alive and not petrified, because a killing blow prevents the change.

FromToMinimum attributesTriggered by
GolemStone GolemStrength 104, Vitality 129Gaze of Terror, Petrify, or a hit from Ji’ylga’s Bow
Stone GolemBaldr GolemStrength 144, Vitality 185Plasma Ball or Plasma Storm
ZombieSkeletonNoneAny Flame damage
SkeletonGhostNonePlasma Ball or Plasma Storm

Golem minimums use the Golem’s own attributes without equipment bonuses. Training battles block all four changes, and so do some story conditions.

Golems

A qualifying Golem hit by Gaze of Terror turns into a Stone Golem instead of turning to stone, as long as Gaze of Terror itself succeeds. With Petrify, the spell only has to hit and the Golem survive, because Petrify’s own chance to petrify doesn’t matter. Ji’ylga’s Bow works on any hit the Golem survives.

Undead

For a Zombie, “Flame damage” includes Fire Breath, Crimson Note, Fireball, Fire Storm, Salamander, and Fire Blast, as well as hits from Flame weapons. A Skeleton needs Plasma Ball or Plasma Storm specifically. Ordinary Wind lightning won’t do it, and neither will Ray of Paralysis or Bind Flare, even though they share an element.

Your own Zombie also needs a Halt Hammer and Torn Cloth to become a Skeleton. Each counts if it’s a default, already worn, or a spare. A Skeleton’s defaults already include the Torn Cloth that Ghost needs, and Golems need no equipment. Enemies skip the equipment check, and the check never uses items up.

What the change keeps

The character keeps their current HP, maximum HP, level, attributes, Luck, Alignment, and name. Unlike after-battle evolution, custom equipment is replaced with the new class’s defaults. Named characters may get defaults tied to their identity.

Changes after a scenario

After the scenario rewards are paid, each fallen character on your roster may come back as an Angel Knight or a Zombie. This happens only at the end of a scenario, not after every battle, and the character doesn’t have to be in a deployed squad.

Squad leaders never transform. The characters who can are Fighters and the human classes from Amazon through Centurion, along with some special versions of classes, while Soldiers, Lycanthropes, Angel Knights, and existing undead can’t. Fallen women first try to become an Angel Knight. Fallen men, and women whose Angel Knight attempt fails, then roll to become a Zombie.

Becoming an Angel Knight

  1. Spare equipment. You need one spare Needle of Light, Plate Mail, and Kite Shield that nobody is wearing. Items the fallen character wears don’t count. Characters are checked in roster order, so an earlier one can claim the spares first.
  2. Attributes and Alignment. The character needs Intelligence 60, Mentality 61, and Dexterity 57 or higher, from their permanent attributes, and Alignment 50–100. There’s no level requirement.
  3. A Luck roll. The chance is roughly Luck ÷ 4 percent, so Luck 40 gives about 10% and Luck 100 about 25%.

If any step fails, the character goes on to the Zombie roll. A successful Angel Knight never becomes a Zombie.

Becoming a Zombie

The Zombie chance is 30%. A Mastaba’s Barrier carried by a squad protects its members from becoming Zombies. It isn’t used up, and it doesn’t stop Angel Knights. Because of a bug, it can sometimes protect one character outside that squad as well. Angel’s Brooch has no effect on either change.

After the change

The character keeps their name, level, experience, maximum HP, attributes, Luck, and Alignment, and returns at full HP. They stay on the roster, so no free slot is needed. Their custom equipment choices are cleared and they wear the new class’s defaults. An Angel Knight equips the three spares, and a Zombie gets Old Clothing, which can’t be added if you have none and your inventory is full.

Most of the old equipment goes back into your inventory. Sonic Blade, Hemlock, Dream Tiara, Blue Sash, and Tunic are exceptions: those copies are lost, and some custom equipment can be lost the same way.

At the end of each scenario, the game also restores every Zombie, Skeleton, and Ghost to full HP without changing their class.

Class-change glossary

Evolution

An automatic class change that you don’t choose from the menu. Evolution happens after battle, when an attack strikes certain monsters, or when a scenario ends.

End-of-battle attributes

The attributes a character has when the battle ends, including any Power Up, Power Down, or Poison, unless they levelled up in that battle. After-battle evolution checks these, not the new class’s starting values.

Spare equipment

An item you own that nobody is wearing. An item worn by another character isn’t a spare.

Named characters

Some named characters keep their own identity while their class changes, so they keep their name and any special equipment tied to them.

Modder reference: Automatic Class Changes

Automatic class changes run through four separate routes, each with its own data and code. After-battle evolution reads a 16-row table. Attack conversion reads a 5-row table. Soldier graduation and the scenario-end Angel Knight and Zombie changes are mostly code. The two tables are plain, uncompressed ROM data outside the CRC region, and neither is exposed in the Editor yet.

Where these facts come from

Every location and value on this tab was read from the US retail ROM, and offsets are z64. None of the suggested edits has been tried in a running game yet, so test each one from a cold boot before relying on it.

How to read the code and byte evidence

ROM offsets use big-endian z64 order. The master v64 stores each byte pair in reverse order. RAM addresses belong to the stated overlay or structure.

Each code line shows the z64 offset, the four original bytes, and the MIPS instruction. Relative branches name z64 destinations; J/JAL targets are encoded RAM addresses. The instruction after a branch is its delay slot.

Samples are stored bytes, not calculated values. For compressed resources, the sample gives the container’s ROM offset and the offset inside the decoded file.

Evolution table

Sixteen 11-byte rows define every after-battle evolution. The selector scans them in order and uses the first row that matches, which is how Platinum Dragon and Black Dragon take priority over the elemental dragons.

Location
z64 0x00228E68 + 11 × row (RAM 0x801E5B98 while the combat overlay is loaded).
Layout
+0 source class · +1 target class · +2 Element · +3–+8 minimum STR, VIT, INT, MEN, AGI, DEX · +9 minimum Alignment · +10 maximum Alignment
Row 0
38 3D 08 00 72 49 65 00 00 46 64: Young Dragon → Platinum Dragon, any Element, VIT 114, INT 73, MEN 101, Alignment 70–100.
Row 15
24 25 08 00 00 6C 7D 00 79 4B 64: Angel Knight → Seraph, INT 108, MEN 125, DEX 121, Alignment 75–100.
In the Editor
Not exposed.

How to change it

Edit the minima or Alignment bytes in place. To lower Seraph’s MEN requirement to 100, change 0x00228F13 from 7D to 64. To add a new evolution, replace a row you don’t need; the table has no spare slots.

Watch out for

  • Moving rows changes which evolution wins when several match.
  • The target class’s default equipment must be available, or the row fails; see Evolution selector.
  • These rows don’t affect class changes from the menu.

Evolution selector

For each character, the selector scans the 16 rows in order. It checks secondary class, Element, the six minima against current battle attributes, and Alignment. At the first match, it also checks that the target’s default equipment is available. If that equipment check fails, it returns no evolution without trying later rows.

Code
func_00219730 (z64 0x00219730–0x00219A14), running at RAM 0x801D6460.
Actor fields
Attributes +0x24–+0x2E · Element +0x33 · Alignment +0x34 · secondary class +0x4C. Level (+0x31) isn’t read.
Equipment rule
Each nonzero target default must be in the inventory. It passes if it’s a source-class default or currently worn, or else if equipped < owned for that item.

Watch out for

  • Battle attributes include Power and Poison, but a level-up earlier in the results reloads saved attributes first.
  • The availability check never changes item counts.

Applying evolution

This routine scans the 20 actor slots. It skips dead, petrified, enemy, Soldier, and already-evolved actors, then builds a replacement actor with the new class. The replacement copies HP, attributes, Luck, level, experience, Element, Alignment, and equipment, and is marked as evolved so it can’t evolve again this battle.

Code
func_00219F0C (z64 0x00219F0C–0x0021A438), running at RAM 0x801D6C3C.
Class write
If primary and secondary class were equal, both become the target; otherwise only the secondary does. The same rule is written to the roster.
Equipment
The four saved equipment overrides are kept. A zero override means “class default” and later resolves to the new class’s default.

Watch out for

  • Old gear can still show during the battle; the equipment recount happens at teardown.
  • What happens when all 20 actor slots are full hasn’t been worked out.

Battle results order

Battle results run in phases. Phase 5 handles Alignment, experience, and levels. Phase 8 (graduation) runs before phase 7 (evolution). Training and scripted preservation skip evolution.

Attack conversion table

Five 5-byte rows define the mid-battle conversions. Each gives a source and target class, minimum permanent STR and VIT, and the trigger that must hit.

Location
z64 0x00239D48 + 5 × row (RAM 0x801F6A78 while loaded).
Rows
4E 4F 68 81 00 Golem → Stone Golem, STR 104, VIT 129, petrification · 4F 50 90 B9 01 Stone → Baldr Golem, STR 144, VIT 185, Plasma · 2D 2F 00 00 02 and 2E 2F 00 00 02 Zombie → Skeleton, Flame · 2F 30 00 00 01 Skeleton → Ghost, Plasma
In the Editor
Not exposed.

How to change it

To make Plasma turn Zombies into Ghosts, change row 2’s target and trigger at 0x00239D53 and 0x00239D56 to 30 and 01, and do the same for row 3. Minima use permanent attributes without equipment.

Watch out for

  • Trigger 1 means Plasma Ball or Plasma Storm specifically; ordinary Wind lightning doesn’t reach this route.
  • Your own characters still need the target’s default equipment to be available.

Graduation check

Once the leader’s progress is 100 or more, this check writes 99 before testing everything else. A later failure therefore leaves progress at 99, and a successful graduation resets it to 0.
