Fewer than 94 occupied character records, spare starter equipment, and no training, neutral encounter, or blocking formation or story state.

How to change it

Lowering the threshold means changing both the comparison and the early write of 99.

Watch out for

  • Progress gain is calculated elsewhere, with its own victory, leader, formation, and mode checks.

Building a graduate

The constructor makes a new roster record at the scenario’s Soldier starting level. It generates a Fighter or Amazon with a new name and attributes, moves them into the Soldier’s formation slot, and resets progress. Nothing is copied from the Soldier’s attributes.

Scenario-end Angel Knight and Zombie

At scenario end, this selector scans fallen roster entries whose class flags allow it. For a woman, it tests three spare items, INT 60, MEN 61, DEX 57, Alignment 50–100, and then rand() % 400 < Luck. If any of that fails, or for a man, it rolls rand() % 10 < 3 for a Zombie, which Mastaba’s Barrier can block.

Code
func_001B6538 (z64 0x001B6538–0x001B7414).
Random range
rand() returns 0–32,767, so the % 400 remainders aren’t perfectly even. Luck 40 passes on 3,280 of 32,768 values, just over 10%.
Skipped
Scenario key 54 bypasses this route, and squad leaders are excluded.
Eligibility
Both class fields must have flag 10; see Class flags for death changes.

How to change it

The 400, the 10, the 3, and the INT/MEN/DEX minimums are constants in this function.

Watch out for

  • Spares are claimed in roster order, so an earlier character can use them up.
  • Some items are destroyed rather than returned when equipment is cleared (Sonic Blade, Hemlock, Dream Tiara, Blue Sash, Tunic).

Class flags for death changes

One byte per class decides who can transform at scenario end. Bit 10 allows it and bit 20 allows the character’s identity to be replaced. The same bytes hold the status immunity bits in 01–08, so this is the table described on the Status effects tab.

Location
z64 0x008ACB32 + class ID − 1, 164 uncompressed bytes (resource 0x003188AE).
Example
Classes 1–8: 08 30 00 30 30 30 30 30. Soldier (08) can’t transform, Fighter and Amazon (30) can, and Lycanthrope (00) can’t.
In the Editor
Not exposed.

How to change it

To let a class transform at scenario end, OR 10 into its byte. Keep its immunity bits as they are.

Watch out for

  • Both the primary and secondary class must carry 10.
  • Don’t use the old zombichk.bin extraction; it doesn’t match the retail bytes.

This routine counts eligible fallen characters. It builds a protection mask from item 0x1E (Mastaba’s Barrier) carried by each character’s first matching squad. The mask uses 32-bit shifts, so some roster IDs share a bit: 1 with 33, and so on through 31 with 63, and 64 with 96 through 67 with 99.

Class record: level history

Bytes B53–B57 of each class record say which class a character counted as at earlier levels. They describe history, not an unlock, and they don’t take part in automatic evolution.

Location
Class record at z64 0x0005DAD8 + (class ID + 1) × 72.
Layout
B34–B41 default equipment (four u16) · B53 first predecessor · B54 its level threshold (FF = none) · B55 second predecessor · B56 its threshold · B57 class-copy match ID
Example
Paladin at 0x0005E0AD: 02 06 05 0F 00 means Fighter below level 6, then Knight below 15, then Paladin.
In the Editor
Classes tab.

Watch out for

  • The physical record index is class ID + 1.
  • B57 is a class-copy match, not an item or quest requirement.

CHARACTER & CAMPAIGN

Experience and levelling

Where experience comes from, why some battles pay far more than others, and how levels are gained.

When a battle ends, each of your characters who is still standing earns experience for every enemy the squad defeated, not just the ones they defeated personally. Enemies above your level are worth far more, large monsters are worth half again as much, and the total is split between everyone who survived.

How experience works

  • Everyone shares. Each surviving character gets experience for every enemy defeated in the battle, whoever landed the blow.
  • Tough enemies pay much more. An enemy’s value is (level gap + 8) squared, so it climbs steeply with every level it has over you.
  • Survivors split it. The bigger the surviving squad, the smaller each share, and Soldiers take a share without earning any experience themselves.
  • 100 XP is one level. Anything over 100 is lost, and a character can gain only one level per battle.

How much you get

For each character, the game adds up the value of every enemy defeated in the battle:

Each enemy is worth (enemy level − your level + 8)², minimum 1
× 1.5 for a large monster, × 0.8 for a Soldier
÷ the number of characters sharing
 
Experience = total, rounded up, between 1 and 100 (0 if nothing was defeated)
+ 1 battle bonus (not in training or some story battles)
then capped at 100

The level comparison is made separately for each of your characters, so in the same battle a low-level character earns far more than a high-level one. Characters sharing means everyone on your side who is alive and not petrified when the battle ends. That includes Soldiers, even though Soldiers never earn experience themselves.

The +1 battle bonus means every surviving character earns at least 1 XP from any real battle, even one in which nothing was defeated. Training battles don’t give the bonus.

Manual of Warfare

A Manual of Warfare carried by the squad doubles experience. It doubles the enemies’ total before rounding, and it raises the battle bonus to 2, but the 100 cap still applies. A total of 4.2, for example, becomes 5 + 1 = 6 without the Manual and 9 + 2 = 11 with it.

What makes an enemy worth more

Two things decide an enemy’s value: its level compared with yours, and its size. The class otherwise makes no difference.

One regular enemy

Enemy level compared with yoursPoints before sharing
7 or more below1
6 below4
5 below9
4 below16
3 below25
2 below36
1 below49
Same level64
1 above81
2 above100
3 above121
4 above144
5 above169
10 above324

The value is (level gap + 8) squared, so defeating an enemy 2 levels above you is worth about 1.6 times as much as one at your level, and one 5 levels above is worth over 2.5 times. Enemies 7 or more levels below you are worth almost nothing. An enemy counts only if it ends the battle at 0 HP, so a petrified enemy that still has HP gives nothing.

Size

EnemyMultiplier
Large monsters: Ogre, Young Dragon, Thunder Dragon, Red Dragon, Earth Dragon, Blue Dragon, Platinum Dragon, Black Dragon, Quetzalcoatl, Flarebrass, Ahzi Dahaka, Hydra, Bahamut, Tiamat, Wyrm, Wyvern, Griffin, Opinincus, Cockatrice, Sphinx, Hellhound, Cerberus, Golem, Stone Golem, Baldr Golem, Death Bahamut× 1.5
Soldiers× 0.8
Every other class, including Giants and all humans× 1.0

Undead destroyed outright by a holy attack still count, as regular-size enemies. See Status effects.

Worked example

A squad of five fights and nobody falls. It defeats three level-10 Fighters and a level-12 Wyrm, which is large. Everyone in the squad shares between 5.

EnemyFor a level-10 characterFor a level-14 character
Each level-10 Fighter(10 − 10 + 8)² = 64 ÷ 5 = 12.8(10 − 14 + 8)² = 16 ÷ 5 = 3.2
Three Fighters38.49.6
Level-12 Wyrm(12 − 10 + 8)² = 100 ÷ 5 × 1.5 = 30(12 − 14 + 8)² = 36 ÷ 5 × 1.5 = 10.8
Total68.4, rounded up to 6920.4, rounded up to 21
Plus battle bonus70 XP22 XP

With a Manual of Warfare, the level-10 character would get 100 (68.4 × 2 = 136.8 is capped at 100 before the bonus, and the total is capped again), and the level-14 character 41 + 2 = 43. A level-1 character in the same squad would reach the 100 cap easily, but could still gain only one level.

Levelling up

Experience is checked at the end of each battle. A character who reaches 100 gains one level, and their experience resets to 0. Anything above 100 is lost rather than carried over, and no character gains more than one level from a single battle. Characters at level 99 earn nothing.

A Champion Statuette also gives one level immediately. It doesn’t use or reset the character’s experience.

What each level adds is covered in Attribute growth. Levelling up happens before the after-battle evolution check, which matters if a monster was relying on a temporary Power Up; see Status effects.

Who gets nothing

CharacterExperience
Fallen in battleNone, but earlier progress is kept
PetrifiedNone, and not counted in the share
SoldiersNone, but they are counted in the share
Level 99None
EnemiesEnemies never earn experience

In ordinary battles you earn experience for the enemies you defeated even if you don’t win. In training battles, experience is awarded only when you win, and the +1 battle bonus doesn’t apply. Some story battles follow the training rule too.

Tips

  • Bring weaker characters along. They earn far more from the same enemies than your strongest characters do.
  • Soldiers cost experience. Every Soldier in a squad takes a share without using it, so a squad without Soldiers levels faster.
  • Fight up. An enemy a few levels above you is worth one and a half to two and a half times as much as one at your level.
  • Carry a Manual of Warfare in the squad you most want to level.
  • Watch the cap. Experience past 100 is wasted, so a character close to levelling gains nothing extra from a huge battle.

Experience glossary

Experience (XP)

Progress toward a character’s next level, from 0 to 99. Reaching 100 raises the level by one and resets the count to 0.

Characters sharing

Every character on your side of the battle who is alive and not petrified when it ends, Soldiers included. Each defeated enemy’s value is divided by this number.

Enemy size

Large monsters are worth 1.5 times as much experience and Soldiers 0.8 times. Every other class, including Giants, counts as regular and is worth the normal amount.

Battle bonus

An extra 1 XP (2 with a Manual of Warfare) given to everyone who earns experience, except in training battles and some story battles.

Modder reference: Experience and levelling

Experience is one byte per character (0–99) and one calculator in the combat overlay. The calculator’s only per-class input is the defeated enemy’s Size byte, chosen through the primary class’s B57 class-copy byte, and the Editor already exposes Size. The Editor’s Tools tab can also scale all Size weights by one percentage. Everything else is a constant in code or a battle-state flag, and there’s no XP table or per-class XP coefficient.

Where these facts come from

Every location and value on this tab was read from the US retail ROM, and offsets are z64. None of the suggested edits has been tried in a running game yet, so test each one from a cold boot before relying on it.

The class records are inside the CRC-checked region (z64 0x1000–0x100FFF); the calculator and constants are outside it. Size also controls formation (a large unit counts as two member slots and keeps adjacent cells empty), so it isn’t an XP-only field.

The exact calculation

StepRule
Sharers (N)Player-side battle actors that are alive and not petrified, Soldiers included
SourcesEnemy-side actors with HP 0 and flag 0x1000 clear, plus queued levels at combat state +0x608E (count +0x608D)
Per sourcet = max(sourceLevel − level + 8, 1); term = f32(t² ÷ N) × weight, where the weight is applied in double precision
Core0 with no sources, otherwise clamp(ceil(sum × manual), 1, 100), where manual is 2 with item 29 and 1 without
Bonusmanual unless Training (0x801976D8 & 0x08) or preservation (0x80197B60 ≠ 0)
Awardclamp(core + bonus, 1, 100), or 0 when both are 0

Recipients must be player-side, alive, not petrified, not a Soldier (secondary class 1), and below level 99. The squad index at 0x801976DC must be below 30.

What do you want to change?

Make experience faster or slower

Use the Tools tab’s Experience Size Weight Scale to scale every enemy’s value, or patch the +8 level-gap offset. There’s no XP table.

See XP calculator

Make an enemy class worth more

Its Size byte is the only per-class input, but Size also changes formation. Changing the weight constants affects every class of that size.

See Class Size · Size weight constants

Change when levels are gained

The 100 threshold and the reset to 0 are in the level pass.

See Award and level-up passes

Read or set a character’s experience

Byte +0x35 of the character record, or the Save Game Editor.

See Saved experience

How to read the code and byte evidence

ROM offsets use big-endian z64 order. The master v64 stores each byte pair in reverse order. RAM addresses belong to the stated overlay or structure.

Each code line shows the z64 offset, the four original bytes, and the MIPS instruction. Relative branches name z64 destinations; J/JAL targets are encoded RAM addresses. The instruction after a branch is its delay slot.

Samples are stored bytes, not calculated values. For compressed resources, the sample gives the container’s ROM offset and the offset inside the decoded file.

XP calculator

func_002190AC works out one character’s award. It first collects the queued source levels, then scans the 20 battle actors, counting living, non-petrified player actors as sharers and taking every enemy at 0 HP as a source. It rejects ineligible recipients, sums each source’s term in single precision, applies the Manual of Warfare, rounds up, clamps, adds the bonus, and clamps again.

Code
func_002190AC (z64 0x002190AC–0x00219470), running at RAM 0x801D5DDC.
Level-gap offset
addiu $v0, $v0, 0x8 at z64 0x002192B8.
Clamp constants
1.0 (0x3F80) and 100.0 (0x42C8) are loaded with lui at 0x0021934C, 0x0021936C, 0x002193E0, and 0x002193FC.
Actor fields
HP +0x20 · level +0x31 · experience +0x32 · flags +0x40 · class pair +0x4B/+0x4F
Helpers
Dead func_0020C2C0 · petrified func_0020C32C · player side func_0020C014 · enemy side func_0020BFF8 · Soldier func_0020C104 · flag 0x1000 func_0020C0CC

How to change it

To give more experience from low-level enemies, raise the +8 offset. For example, 0x0A makes an equal-level enemy worth 100 points instead of 64.

Raising the 100.0 cap has no levelling effect, because anything above 100 is discarded at the level pass. The award is also added to a byte, so any cap must stay at 156 or below to avoid wrapping.

Watch out for

  • Soldiers count as sharers even though they can’t receive experience, so they dilute everyone else’s share.
  • Actors with the paired-construction flag 0x1000 (meaning still open) aren’t sources.
  • Queued sources always use weight 1.0 because only their level is stored.
  • The source list is 8 entries on the stack (levels at sp+0x10, Sizes at sp+0x18). A ninth source would overwrite the Size entries; retail battles stay within 8.
  • The Tools tab’s Experience Size Weight Scale patches 0x0021928C, 0x002192BC, and 0x002192F8. Hand edits between 0x0021928C and 0x00219323 will conflict with it.

Award and level-up passes

Battle results run a small state machine at combat state +0x6048. The award pass calls the calculator for every living player-side actor and adds the award to +0x32. In Training or scripted preservation it runs only when the outcome field +0x6068 is 0; otherwise it runs regardless of outcome. The level pass then takes each living, non-Soldier player actor at 100 or more, sets +0x32 to 0, and runs export, the level increase, and a reload.

Code
func_00219470 (z64 0x00219470–0x00219730): award loop at 0x0021954C, level pass at 0x002195FC.
Level increase
func_0021C140 (export), then func_00044AA4 (growth, on the character record), then func_0021C074 (reload).
Order
Alignment settling runs first, then experience, then levels, and after-battle evolution comes later.
All level-gain callers
This level pass (0x00219678), the Champion Statuette (0x00041324), combat playback opcode 0x37 (0x00220A60), and the character initializer (0x00045338).

How to change it

The 100 threshold is sltiu $v0, $v0, 0x64 at z64 0x0021964C. A three-word patch carries the excess over instead of discarding it:

0x0021964C → 2443FF9C (addiu $v1, $v0, -0x64); 0x00219650 → 04620012 (bltzl $v1, same target); 0x00219660 → A2030032 (sb $v1, 0x32($s0)). The store sits in the delay slot before export, so the remainder survives into the saved record.

Watch out for

  • Each actor is visited once per pass, so no one can gain two levels from one battle. Raising the award cap won’t change that.
  • Presentation events (0x11 for the award, 0x0C for a level) are queued here, so the on-screen results follow these values.
  • Combat playback also has opcode 0x35, which adds +0xA5 to +0x32 with no cap, and opcode 0x37, which runs a level-up. No emitter for either has been traced in retail.
  • Some battle endings request a different results phase and skip this state entirely, so not every exit awards experience.

Class Size

The source’s Size comes from its class pair. The resolver uses the primary class’s Size if primary B57 equals the secondary class ID, and the secondary class’s Size otherwise, so named characters in special class versions use the right record. Size 0 weighs 0.8, Size 2 weighs 1.5, and anything else weighs 1.0.

Location
z64 0x0005DB18 + 72 × class ID (the name/header origin + 4, or the stats origin − 8).
Retail values
Only Soldier (1) is 0. 26 classes are 2: Ogre, the dragons, the Wyrm to Cerberus beasts, the three Golems, and Death Bahamut. Giant (77) is 1.
Code
func_00043D1C (resident), running at RAM 0x8016DE1C.
In the Editor
Classes tab, Size.

Watch out for

  • Size is also the formation size: a large unit counts as two member slots and keeps adjacent cells empty. Changing Size to adjust experience changes formation too.

Size weight constants

The two non-default weights are IEEE doubles in the combat overlay’s data. The calculator multiplies each term by one of them after converting to double, then converts back to single precision.

Location
z64 0x002299A0: 3FE999999999999A (0.8) then 3FF8000000000000 (1.5). Loaded from RAM 0x801E66D0 and 0x801E66D8.

How to change it

To make large monsters worth double, change the second double to 4000000000000000 (2.0).

Watch out for

  • Check that nothing else loads these two doubles before changing them. Only this use is traced.

Manual of Warfare

func_0020F9AC returns true if any of the ten carried-item bytes of the squad in battle equals the item ID passed in. The calculator asks for item 29 twice: once to double the raw sum before rounding, and once to double the bonus.

Squad record
RAM 0x801971F0 + 25 × squad, carried items at +0x0D–+0x16. The squad index is at 0x801976DC.
Code
func_0020F9AC (z64 0x0020F9AC–0x0020FA04), running at RAM 0x801CC51C. The same helper checks other carried items too, such as Medal of Vigor (0x18).

How to change it

The item ID is the addiu $a0, $zero, 0x1D immediate at z64 0x00219338 and 0x002193AC in the calculator.

Holy-removed enemies

When battle event 0x31 removes an undead character outright, the actor is gone before results, so the 0-HP scan can’t see it. For an enemy, the event appends its level to combat state +0x608E and increments the count at +0x608D, and the calculator adds these as weight-1.0 sources. For a player undead, it instead increments a halfword counter at 0x80196A70, capped at 9,999.

Code
func_0021EBBC, z64 0x00220298–0x002202EC.
Reset
The count is cleared at battle start in func_002152FC (z64 0x00215374).
Training and preservation
The handler still zeroes the target’s HP and sets its dead flag (0x00220254–0x00220268) before the Training check. It then skips the queue, the counter, and the removal, so the enemy stays in its slot and counts through the normal 0-HP scan at its real Size.

Watch out for

  • What the 0x80196A70 counter is used for isn’t known.

Saved experience

Experience lives in character record byte +0x35. At battle start, func_0021C074 copies it into actor +0x32. Afterwards, the batch writeback (func_0021C3B0) and the level path (func_0021C140) copy +0x32 back.

Import
func_0021C074, z64 0x0021C118–0x0021C11C.
Writeback
func_0021C3B0, z64 0x0021C520–0x0021C528; level path func_0021C140, 0x0021C2BC–0x0021C2C0.
In the Editor
Save Game Editor.

Watch out for

  • Keep saved values at 0–99. A value of 100 or more levels up at the end of the next battle the character survives (not as a Soldier), and values of 156 or more can wrap when the award is added.

CHARACTER & CAMPAIGN

Attribute growth

What each level adds, why the class you level in matters, and which equipment makes levels count for more.

Every level raises maximum HP and the six main attributes by a fixed amount for the character’s current class, plus a small random bonus. Luck never rises from levelling. Because growth follows the class you are in when the level arrives, the order in which you change classes shapes a character for good.

How growth works

  • Growth follows your current class. A level gained as a Knight grows like a Knight, however the character started. A few story characters level using a related class’s record; see the story table below.
  • Each gain is the class amount plus 0, 1, or 2. On average a level adds the class amount + 1 to each attribute.
  • Some equipment adds more. Growth equipment adds points to certain attributes at every level, and those points stay after the item comes off.
  • Luck doesn’t grow. No retail class or equipment raises Luck when levelling.
  • Levels don’t heal. Maximum HP rises, but current HP stays where it was.

What a level adds

Each level raises maximum HP, STR, VIT, INT, MEN, AGI, and DEX. Every one of the seven follows the same rule:

Gain = class growth + random 0 or 1 + random 0 or 1 + equipment growth
Attributes and maximum HP stop at 999; level stops at 99.

The two random bonuses are rolled separately for each attribute, so any gain can come out at the class amount, one more, or two more, and the average is the class amount + 1. A Fighter, for example, has STR growth 3, so each level adds 3–5 STR and 4 on average.

Soldiers are the exception. They skip the random bonuses and always gain exactly their class amount + 1, plus any growth equipment.

Luck isn’t part of the rule. Only equipment can raise Luck at a level, and no retail item does, so a character’s Luck changes only through items like the Goblet of Destiny. Alignment isn’t affected either, and current HP isn’t refilled. See Experience and levelling for how levels are earned.

Champion Statuette

Using a Champion Statuette gives one level immediately, with exactly the same growth as a level earned in battle. The character’s current experience is left as it was.

Some equipment adds growth to one or more attributes every time its wearer gains a level; Firecrest raises all seven. Only what is equipped at the moment of the level-up counts, default equipment included, and the extra points are permanent.

Characters the game creates

Characters the game creates at a set level, such as enemy squads, wild monsters, your starting roster, and Soldier graduates, don’t get fixed stats. The game starts from the level-1 values of the first class in their class history and replays every level-up (randomly, except for Soldiers), following that history. A Paladin created at level 20, for example, grows as a Fighter for its early levels, then as a Knight, then as a Paladin, switching at the level limits in the Paladin’s class history (6 and 15).

That’s why two enemies of the same class and level can have slightly different attributes. Created characters start at full HP, and their Luck is set to their class’s value. See Soldier graduation.

Tips

  • Plan the order of class changes. Growth depends on the class at each level-up, so spending levels in a class with strong growth in the attributes you want pays off permanently.
  • Level with growth gear on. Equip growth items before a battle you expect to level in; the bonus applies only at the moment of the level-up.
  • Soldiers are predictable. Their gains never vary, so a Soldier’s attributes at a given level are always the same unless items changed them.
  • Temporary boosts don’t help growth. Power Up and Poison change battle attributes, not what a level adds, and a level-up in battle reloads the permanent values; see Status effects.

Growth glossary

Class growth

A fixed amount stored for each class and attribute. Each level adds it plus a random 0–2, so the average gain is the class growth + 1.

Growth equipment

Equipment that adds extra points to certain attributes every time its wearer gains a level. The points stay after the item is removed.

Current class

The class a character belongs to at the moment they level up. Growth always uses this class, not the class they started in.

Modder reference: Attribute growth

Level growth is one resident routine reading two tables: the class records (a growth byte per attribute) and the item records (two-bit growth lanes). Both tables are already editable in the Editor. The same routine runs for a level earned in battle, for a Champion Statuette, and once per level when the game builds a character at a set level.

Where these facts come from

Every location and value on this tab was read from the US retail ROM, and offsets are z64. The level-gain writer also has accepted matching C. None of the suggested edits has been tried in a running game yet, so test each one from a cold boot before relying on it.

What do you want to change?

Change how fast a class grows

Edit its growth bytes in the Classes tab. Each level adds the byte plus 0–2.

See Class growth bytes · Level-gain writer

Make an item add growth

Set a lane in its B20/B21 bytes. Lane values run 0–3.

See Equipment growth lanes

Change the randomness, or give Luck growth

Item Luck growth is a data edit (the B21 Luck lane). Class-based Luck growth and changes to the randomness need a code patch.

See Level-gain writer · Equipment growth lanes · Random-number generator

Understand how enemies and recruits get their stats

The initializer replays one level-gain per level along the class history.

See Character initializer

How to read the code and byte evidence

ROM offsets use big-endian z64 order. The master v64 stores each byte pair in reverse order. RAM addresses belong to the stated overlay or structure.

Each code line shows the z64 offset, the four original bytes, and the MIPS instruction. Relative branches name z64 destinations; J/JAL targets are encoded RAM addresses. The instruction after a branch is its delay slot.

Samples are stored bytes, not calculated values. For compressed resources, the sample gives the container’s ROM offset and the offset inside the decoded file.

Level-gain writerClass growth bytesEquipment growth lanesCharacter initializerRandom-number generatorChampion Statuette

Level-gain writer

func_00044AA4 takes a character record. If the level is below 99 it adds one level, reads the runtime class record for the secondary class (+0x12), and adds to each of max HP and the six attributes the class growth + rand() % 2 + rand() % 2 + equipment lanes. Soldiers (class 1) get a fixed +1 instead of the two random bits. Luck gets only its equipment lane. Results are capped at 999, and Luck is clamped to 0–100.

Code
func_00044AA4 (z64 0x00044AA4–0x0004501C), resident at RAM 0x8016EBA4; accepted matching C func_00044aa4.c.
Class records read
RAM 0x80187C14 + 72 × class (the runtime copy of the name-origin records).
Caps
Level sltiu … 0x63 at 0x00044ADC; 999 (0x3E7) from 0x00044EE8; Luck 100 (0x64) at 0x00044FE4.
Callers
Battle level-up (func_00219470), combat playback’s level event (func_0021EBBC), Champion Statuette (func_00041098), and the initializer (func_0004501C).
Not changed
Current HP +0x18, Alignment +0x1B, experience +0x35.

How to change it

Class and item changes need no code. To give every class the Soldier’s fixed +1 instead of the random 0–2, make each Soldier test always taken: replace the beql at 0x00044B10, 0x00044B68, 0x00044BC0, 0x00044C14, 0x00044C68, 0x00044CBC, and 0x00044D10 with 50000010 (beql $zero, $zero). Their delay slot addiu $s0, $zero, 1 supplies the +1. Replacing the rand calls with constants doesn’t work, because the second call’s delay slot copies the first result.

Watch out for

  • Growth bytes are unsigned, so FF means 255, not ‘no growth’. Giant (77) and the special story classes store FF in every field.
  • Natural levels use the record at +0x12. Normal builders set it to the primary class’s B57 when that byte is nonzero, so several named characters level using another record. Vad levels as Grappler 0x72, Amazeroth and Vapula as Temple Cmdr (Pruflas) 0x69, Kerikov and Count Silvis as Vanity (Godeslas) 0x6C, and the named enemy leaders 0x89–0xA2 as their generic classes. Edit that record. Stats built by the initializer instead follow the named record’s own class history.

Class growth bytes

Each class record stores an initial value and a growth byte for max HP and each attribute. Luck has an initial value but no growth byte. The unused bytes between them (stats origin +3, +7, +11, +15, +19) aren’t read by growth and should be left alone.

Example
Fighter: HP 00 46 04 (70, growth 4); STR 00 32 03 (50, growth 3).
Retail ranges
HP 2–7, STR 1–6, VIT 1–6, INT 1–6, MEN 2–5, AGI 1–5, DEX 1–6, leaving out records whose growth bytes are all FF.
In the Editor
Classes tab (growth columns).

How to change it

Raise a growth byte to make every level in that class add more. Keep the other bytes in the record unchanged.

Equipment growth lanes

Item bytes B20 and B21 pack eight two-bit lanes, each 0–3. The writer resolves all four equipment slots, using class defaults for empty overrides, and adds each item’s lanes. Every retail lane value is 1, and no retail item uses the Luck lane.

Location
z64 0x00062310 + 32 × item + 20 (B20) and +21 (B21).
Retail items
35 items have a nonzero lane. 30 add growth. Five (Ogre Blade, Heavy Axe, Ogre Shield, Ogre Armor, Ogre Helm) set only the unused lane, and Firecrest sets the unused lane plus all seven effective lanes.
Accessors
func_000457E4–func_000458B8. The bits 5:4 accessor func_00045800 has no caller, and no code other than the lane accessors reads B20.

How to change it

To give an item +1 Luck per level, OR 01 into its B21. For +2 VIT, clear B21 bits 5:4 (AND CF) and then OR 20.

Watch out for

  • The Luck lane is added on a natural level, but the initializer overwrites Luck with the class value, so characters created at a level lose Luck-lane gains.

Character initializer

func_0004501C builds a character at a requested level. It picks the level-1 class from the class history (B53–B57), copies that class’s initial values, then runs the level-gain writer once per later level. For each level, it temporarily writes the applicable history class into both class fields and restores them afterwards. It then sets current HP to max and writes the class Luck.

Code
func_0004501C (z64 0x0004501C–0x000453E0), resident at RAM 0x8016F11C. Level loop 0x00045298–0x00045350; class restore and full HP 0x00045354–0x00045360.
Callers
Enemy squad builder func_0019554C · deployment hub func_001960A8 · graduate constructor func_00213E30 · initial state and Soldier template func_0005AC70 · prepared starting roster func_0006D96C and func_0006DCC4 · Soldier-template refresh func_0007E2E4 · neutral encounter constructor func_0023A3A0 · scratch preview func_0023FDCC · free player slot with a supplied class func_00249290
Starting values
It starts from the level-1 values of the first class in the history (B53 when level 1 is below B54), not the final class.

Watch out for

  • Only the low byte of the requested level is compared, so keep requests to 1–99.
  • Randomness means two characters built from the same class and level can differ.

Random-number generator

The game’s shared RNG is a linear congruential generator. Growth uses rand() % 2 twice per attribute, 14 calls per ordinary level.

Code
rand (z64 0x0002CBCC–0x0002CC00): state = state × 0x4E6D + 0x3039, returns (state >> 16) & 0x7FFF.
State
RAM 0x800C47D0.

Watch out for

  • The RNG is shared with combat and everything else, so a savestate reload replays the same growth only if nothing else has consumed random numbers in between.

Champion Statuette

Item 9 in the character item dispatcher (func_00041098, jump table at RAM 0x8018FE60, z64 0x00065D60) calls the level-gain writer when applied. It is an ordinary level with ordinary growth.

Code
Apply branch at z64 0x00041308–0x00041334. The dispatcher’s check pass ($t1 = 0) returns usable without reading the level and calls rand once (0x00041314).
Experience
The apply branch only calls the writer, so experience +0x35 is unchanged.

Watch out for

  • At level 99 the writer does nothing, and the item’s usability check doesn’t test the level.

CHARACTER & CAMPAIGN

Changing class

What the class-change menu lists, what each class requires, and what the change costs.

A character can change class from army management whenever they meet the new class’s attribute and Alignment minimums and the army can supply the class’s equipment. There is no level requirement. The attributes, level, and experience the character has built up stay the same; what changes is their equipment and how they grow from then on.

How class changes work

  • Every class has minimums. Each attribute listed for a class must be at least the number shown, and Alignment must be inside the class’s range. Level doesn’t matter.
  • Equipment comes with the class. The character switches to the new class’s standard equipment. Anything they need must be worn already, an unused copy, or bought on the spot.
  • You stay in your line. Men move within the Fighter line, women within the Amazon line, and Hawkmen within their own. Lich and Vampire are one-way exits from it.
  • Classes must be discovered. The menu lists only classes somebody in your army has held or qualified for.

Which classes appear

The class-change menu shows the classes of the character’s line. Classes the character can’t take yet are shown greyed out, and so is their current class.

LineClasses in the menu
Fighter line (men)Fighter and every male human class through Centurion, plus Lich and Vampire
Amazon line (women)Amazon and every female human class through Centurion, plus Lich
Hawkman lineHawkman, Vultan, and Raven

A class only appears after it has been discovered. Each time you open army management, the game adds any class that someone in your army currently belongs to, and any class that someone could change into from their current class: the right sex and line, the attributes and Alignment, and at least one owned copy of every piece of its standard equipment. Goth isn’t checked. Once a class has appeared it stays in the list, even if nobody qualifies any more.

Soldiers, Lycanthropes, Werewolves, Angel Knights, Seraphs, undead, and monsters can’t change class from the menu. Any class changes they have happen automatically; see Automatic class changes.

Requirements

A character can take a listed class when all of these hold:

  • Each attribute is at least the class’s minimum. A dash means no minimum.
  • Alignment is inside the class’s range. Both ends count, so Knight’s 40–100 accepts 40 and rejects 39.
  • Every piece of the class’s standard equipment can be supplied, and you have the Goth for anything that must be bought (see the next section).
  • Centurion has two extra conditions; see Special classes.

Level is never checked, and neither is Luck. Growing into a class is purely a matter of the six attributes and Alignment. See Alignment for ways to move a character’s Alignment into range.

Fighter, Amazon, and Hawkman have no minimums, so a character can always return to the first class of their line if the equipment is available.

Equipment and Goth

The game checks each piece of the new class’s standard equipment in turn:

  • Already worn by this character: fine, it stays on.
  • **You own an unused copy:** fine, the character takes it.
  • You own the item but every copy is in use: the game buys another copy for you at the price shown in the tables.
  • You don’t own the item at all: the class can’t be chosen.

The prices of everything that must be bought are added together, and the change is refused if you don’t have that much Goth. The game asks you to confirm before it spends the Goth.

A few items can’t be bought this way at all, so the character must already wear each one or you need an unused copy: Dragoon (Sword of Tiamat and Dragon Armor), Black Knight (Valiant Mantle), Vampire (Count’s Garment and Bloody Emblem), Lich (Ring of the Dead), and Princess (Battle Fan and Dream Tiara).

Because an item you don’t own can’t be bought, one copy of each piece is enough to open a class to your whole army: it lets the class be discovered, and later changes can buy more copies.

Special classes

Centurion

Centurion also needs two things that don’t appear in the table. The character’s leader record must be full, at 99. Each Soldier who graduates from a squad this character leads adds 20 to it, so five graduations fill it; nothing else is known to raise it. A game flag must also be set, and which event sets it isn’t known. See Soldier graduation.

Lich and Vampire

Lich accepts both men and women with low Alignment (0–30) and modest INT and MEN. Vampire is for men only and needs Alignment 0–50. Both need items that can’t be bought, and neither class can change again from the menu, so a Lich or Vampire stays one for good unless something else changes them.

Dragoon, Black Knight, and Princess

These three need equipment that can’t be bought: Dragoon the Sword of Tiamat and Dragon Armor, Black Knight the Valiant Mantle, and Princess the Battle Fan and Dream Tiara. Princess has no attribute minimums at all, only Alignment 70–100.

Named characters

Some named characters join with a special version of an ordinary class. For class changes they count as that ordinary class, which sets their line and requirements.

They keep their name when they change. Changing back to the original class restores their special version, although Europea still has to meet the Centurion conditions to return to Centurion. Characters whose class has no ordinary version, such as Magnus, Dio, Destin, Vad, Saradin, and Biske, can’t change class.

What changes and what doesn’t

After a class changeResult
Level, experience, attributes, HP, AlignmentUnchanged
EquipmentEverything the character wore goes back to your items, and they wear the new class’s standard equipment
Future levelsGrow as the new class; see Attribute growth
GothReduced by the price of any equipment bought

Attributes don’t drop when you move to a class with lower minimums. Returning to a class later means meeting its requirements again, though, and some characters join in a class whose minimums they don’t meet: once they leave it, they can’t come back until they do.

Tips

  • Buy one of everything. Owning a single copy of a class’s gear lets the class be discovered and lets later changes buy extra copies automatically.
  • Spend levels in the class whose growth you want. Changing class doesn’t alter attributes, but every later level grows as the new class.
  • Check Alignment before training. A character outside a class’s Alignment range can’t take it however high their attributes are.
  • Keep unused copies of rare equipment. Items that can’t be bought must already be worn by the character or be unused in your inventory at the moment of the change.
  • Plan Centurions early. Only a leader whose squads produce five graduates qualifies, so pick the leader before the Soldiers start graduating.

Class-change glossary

Class line

The group of classes a character can move between from the menu. Men use the Fighter line, women the Amazon line, and Hawkmen the Hawkman line. Lich, and Vampire for men, can be reached from a line but not left again.

Discovered class

A class the menu has started to list. It is added the first time, on opening army management, that someone in your army belongs to it or could change into it from their current class. It stays listed from then on.

Standard equipment

The weapon, armour, and other gear a class comes with. After a class change the character wears the new class’s standard equipment.

Unused copy

A copy of an item that you own and that isn’t counted as in use. Every character’s standard equipment counts as in use, even when they have swapped a piece for something else.

Modder reference: Changing class

The class-change menu lives in the Army-management overlay. One predicate decides every change; a list builder decides what the menu shows; a refresh decides which classes have been discovered; and a commit routine writes the result. The requirement numbers, class lines, and item flags are all data, so most changes need no code.

Where these facts come from

Every location and value on this tab was read from the US retail ROM, and offsets are z64. Overlay RAM addresses use the Army-overlay delta 0x801135A0. The list builder’s output and the discovered-class bits were checked in the vanilla class-change savestates. None of the suggested edits has been tried in a running game yet, so test each one from a cold boot before relying on it.

Where the data lives

DataLocationFormatIn the Editor
Requirement rowsOB64 LZSS container z64 0x023CDECE81 × 8 bytes: STR, VIT, INT, MEN, AGI, DEX minimums, Alignment min, maxClasses tab (stat gates)
Class linesz64 0x000DBD2C + 2 × classLine nibble + mask byte, FFFF at class 0x51—
Named-class mapz64 0x000DBE18 + classu8 ordinary class, 0 = none—
Standard equipmentClass stats origin +34..+414 × u16 itemClasses tab (equipment)
Item price, can’t-buy flagz64 0x00062310 + 32 × item + 4 and +22 bit 7u16 / bitItems tab
Discovered classesRAM 0x80196A7611 bytes, one bit per class—

The class records, item records, class-line table, and named-map table are all inside the CRC-checked region (z64 0x1000–0x100FFF), so fix the checksum after editing them; the Editor does this on export. The stat-gate container is outside it.

Failure reasons

Code at `*(0x80196AF8) + 0x5ED`Meaning
1Line check failed
2Centurion rule failed
3A standard item with B22 bit 7 has no unused copy
4Not enough Goth for the items to be bought
5Items must be bought while the active task type is 3 (seen in battle states)

Stat and Alignment failures return false without setting a code. A standard item missing from the inventory also sets no code of its own, but the item loop continues, so a later owned-but-unworn item can still store 3 and blame the wrong item.

What do you want to change?

Change a class’s requirements

Edit its stat-gate row. FF in a byte skips that test.

See Stat-gate rows · Class-change predicate

Let a class be bought into without owning its gear

Needs a code change: the predicate and the discovery check both refuse an item that isn’t in the inventory list, and the cost function must price it.

See Standard equipment and cost · Discovered-class bitfield

Make an item purchasable (or not) during a change

Clear or set bit 7 of the item’s B22.

See Standard equipment and cost

Open a class to another line

Edit the class-line table. The list and the line check both read it.

See Class line table · Menu list builder

Let a named character change class

Give their class a named-map entry and set its B57 to the class itself. The map applies only while the secondary class equals B57, and with B57 = 0 the commit overwrites the primary class, losing the character’s identity. B57 also drives the standard-equipment selectors.

See Named-class map · Class-change commit

How to read the code and byte evidence

ROM offsets use big-endian z64 order. The master v64 stores each byte pair in reverse order. RAM addresses belong to the stated overlay or structure.

Each code line shows the z64 offset, the four original bytes, and the MIPS instruction. Relative branches name z64 destinations; J/JAL targets are encoded RAM addresses. The instruction after a branch is its delay slot.

Samples are stored bytes, not calculated values. For compressed resources, the sample gives the container’s ROM offset and the offset inside the decoded file.

Class-change predicateClass line tableMenu list builderDiscovered-class bitfieldStandard equipment and costClass-change commitStat-gate rowsNamed-class map

Class-change predicate

func_000BEDB8(character, class) returns 1 when the menu may change the character to the class. It resolves the current class (the named map when primary B57 equals the secondary class), runs the line check, tests the stat-gate row, supplies the standard equipment, blocks purchases when the active task type is 3, compares the cost with Goth, and applies the Centurion rule for targets 0x22 and 0x23. There is no level test.

Code
z64 0x000BEDB8–0x000BF228, live 0x801D2358.
Stat gates
Row pointer *(*(0x80196AF8) + 0x80) + 8 × class. Bytes 0–5 against character +0x1C…+0x26 (≥), bytes 6–7 bracket Alignment +0x1B (inclusive).
Centurion
Persistent flag 3 (func_00045DF4(3), bank 0x80193686; no direct writer passing 3 has been found) and leader counter +0x36 == 99 (xori …, 0x63 at 0x000BF1C8). Graduation adds 20 to the leader’s +0x36, capped at 99, so five graduations reach 99 if the counter starts at 0; other writers are not ruled out.
Task-type block
u16 at (**(u32 **)0x800C4BBC) + 4 equal to 3, with at least one item to buy, gives reason 5; the test is skipped when that pointer is null. Vanilla savestates read 3 in battle, 5 in army management and on the scenario map, and 2 in world-map management (5 in the Hugo report menu).
Callers
List builder func_000BF248, character counts func_000BF458, func_000BBDAC, func_000C01DC, and the class-change screen func_000CDDF0.

How to change it

To remove the Centurion counter test, replace xori $v1, $v1, 0x0063 at 0x000BF1C8 with addiu $v1, $zero, 0 (24030000); the following sltiu then always yields 1. The discovery check has its own copy at 0x000C3CD4.

Watch out for

  • The same rules are duplicated in the discovery check func_000C3900, which also tests the body code and an owned copy of each item. Change both or the menu and the list disagree. The body-code test (Vampire’s is 0) also stops women discovering Vampire by qualifying.

Class line table

Byte 0’s low nibble is the menu line and byte 1 a compatibility mask. The line check func_000C37EC(current, target) allows a change when the current mask is 1 or 2 with a nonzero line (or current = target) and the masks share a bit, or when the current mask is 8 and both classes are on line 5. Every other current class is refused.

Retail lines
Line 1: Fighter, Knight, Berserker, Fencer, Phalanx, Beast Tamer, Doll Master, Ninja, Wizard, Paladin, Dragoon, Black Knight, Sword Master, Cataphract, Beast Master, Enchanter, Ninja Master, Archmage, Centurion (Male). Line 2: Amazon, Archer, Dragon Tamer, Valkyrie, Witch, Sorceress, Cleric, Diana, Dragon Master, Freya, Siren, Priest, Princess, Centurion (Female). Line 5: Hawkman, Vultan, Raven. Lich is mask 3 with line 0; Vampire mask 1 with line 0.
Consequence
Lich and Vampire can be entered but not left. Lich’s mask 3 is rejected outright by the line check (masks 3 and 4 always fail), and Vampire’s line 0 fails the nonzero-line test. For both, the list builder lists only the current class.

How to change it

To let women become Vampires instead of Liches, change Vampire’s mask to 03 and the line-2 extra test, the delay-slot xori $v0, $s0, 0x0026 at 0x000BF334 (3A020026), to 3A02002B. The xori at 0x000BF358 belongs to the line-1 path. Offering both needs a longer patch.

Menu list builder

func_000BF248 walks the line table and lists classes whose line equals the current line. Line 1 also gets Lich (0x26) and Vampire (0x2B); line 2 gets Lich. Each candidate must have its discovered bit set. The current class is added greyed (| 0x80); for other entries the predicate decides, and lines other than 1, 2, and 5 grey every entry.

Output
*(0x80196AF8) + 0x1C0E (u16 per entry), count at +0x1BFC.
Input class
+0x5E8, set by func_000D0150: the named-map class when primary B57 equals the secondary class, otherwise the secondary class. Classes 0x51 and above take the line-0 path: one greyed entry, the current class.
Savestate check
Vanilla class-change states list Fighter, Knight (greyed, current), and Doll Master (greyed) with discovered bits for Fighter, Amazon, Knight, and Doll Master.

Discovered-class bitfield

Bit class of the 11 bytes at 0x80196A76 must be set before the class appears in the menu. func_000C3DAC, run while army management is set up, sets it, in a first pass over characters 1–99, for each character’s current class (the named-map class whenever map[primary] is nonzero, without the B57 test), and in a second pass over characters 1–98 for every class one of them passes func_000C3900 for. Bits are never cleared by this code.

Discovery check
func_000C3900: the line check, body code (target class record byte = character +0x14, except Lich), stat gates, the Centurion rule, and every standard item present with owned count +3 ≠ 0.
Other readers
func_000BBDAC, func_000BC0BC, func_000BF5DC.

How to change it

To show every class from the start, set the 11 bytes to FF in a save or at new-game initialisation. The predicate still decides what can be chosen.

Standard equipment and cost

For each of the four standard-item selectors, the item passes if the character wears it (func_000BEDB8 calls 0x801D2230) or its inventory entry has in-use below owned. An item with no inventory entry fails. An item whose B22 bit 7 is set and has no unused copy fails with reason 3. Anything else is bought: func_000BF9C8 sums the prices and the predicate compares the sum with Goth.

Inventory
0x80196B00 + 4 × index: u16 item, u8 in use, u8 owned. func_000415FC returns 0x1FF when the item has no entry. The character-release routine func_0004196C zeroes an entry when its owned count reaches 0.
Retail can’t-buy items
Sword of Tiamat, Dragon Armor, Valiant Mantle, Battle Fan, Dream Tiara, Count’s Garment, Bloody Emblem, and Ring of the Dead among menu-class equipment.
Skip
The item loop is skipped when current and target class are equal. The worn test runs before the B22 test and scans all four slots, overrides and class defaults alike, so an unbuyable item the character already wears passes.

How to change it

To allow buying an item the army doesn’t own, redirect the failure path at 0x000BF080–0x000BF084 (j … with move $s1, $zero) to the B22 test at 0x000BF0A8, keeping $s1, and make func_000C3900 and func_000BF9C8 accept the missing entry too. Don’t fall through to 0x000BF088: that reads inventory entry 0x1FF, past the 0x116 real entries. The commit already creates a missing inventory entry.

Class-change commit

On confirmation func_000CDDF0 subtracts the cost from Goth (0x000CEB44–0x000CEB54), releases every item the character wore (0x000CEE8C–0x000CEF60), clears overrides +0x2A…+0x30, writes the class, and then takes each new standard item. When no copy is free it adds an owned copy, creating the inventory entry if needed.

Class write
If the primary class’s B57 is 0, both +0x11 and +0x12 become the target. Otherwise only +0x12 changes: to the target, or to B57 when the target is the named-map class.
Not written
Level, experience, attributes, HP, and Alignment.
After Lich, Vampire, or Vampire (in coffin)
The handler runs an extra step (0x801CFF24) before rebuilding the list.

Stat-gate rows

Eight bytes per class, loaded from an LZSS container when army management opens. Retail human classes use 0 for untested attributes; the code skips bytes equal to FF.

Container

Watch out for

Named-class map

Eleven named party classes map to ordinary classes: Gilbert, Aisha, Europea, Troi, Asnabel, Katreda, Liedel, Sheen, Meredia, Paul, and Carth. Each has B57 pointing to itself, so while they hold their own class the menu treats them as the mapped class.

Unmapped
Magnus (0x51–0x53), Dio, Destin, Saradin, Biske, Vad (B57 = Grappler 0x72), and the named enemy classes 0x89–0xA2 have no entry, so their menu class stays at 0x51 or above and the list holds only the greyed current class.

CHARACTER & CAMPAIGN

Wild monsters and recruiting

Where wild monsters turn up, how to talk them into joining, and which leaders make that easier.

Squads moving across a mission map sometimes run into a lone wild monster. Which monster depends on the mission and the ground the squad is crossing, and it is always at the mission’s standard enemy level. Instead of fighting, you can Talk: the chance it joins depends on your squad leader’s class and on how hurt the monster is.

How wild monsters work

  • Terrain decides the monster. Each mission lists at most one or two monsters per kind of terrain, and rough ground such as forests and highlands produces far more encounters than roads.
  • The monster’s level is fixed by the mission. It matches the mission’s standard enemy level, not your army’s.
  • Talk can recruit it. A leader of a matching class, such as a Dragon Master for dragons, gives the best odds, and most monsters are easier to win over once they are hurt.
  • Push too hard and it runs. Most monsters run away once their HP falls to a set share of their maximum.

When they appear

The game keeps checking for encounters while your squads march across the map. Each check has two steps, and both must pass.

  • The mode check. First comes one roll for the whole map. Its chance depends on whether you are playing the mission itself or exploring a cleared map in Area Investigation.
  • The terrain check. If the mode check passes, the game takes your moving squads in random order and gives each one a roll for the terrain it is standing on. The first squad to succeed meets a monster, and the check ends there.

The mode check

ModeMode checkAbout
Mission11 in 72,0001 in 6,545
Area Investigation51 in 72,0001 in 1,412

Area Investigation passes the mode check 4.6 times as often as a mission.

The terrain check

TerrainTerrain chance
Roads10%
Plains15%
Barrens30%
Forests40%
Marshes30%
Highlands50%
Snowy Plains5%
Snowy Barrens35%
Snowy Forests45%
Snowy Highlands55%

Other terrain never produces encounters. If someone in a squad has a Decoy Cap equipped, that squad’s terrain chance is doubled, which makes Highlands and Snowy Highlands a certainty. The Decoy Cap only helps the squad wearing it. A mission can have monsters on some terrains and none on others, so the terrain chance only matters where the table below lists a monster.

Put together, the chance that one check produces an encounter is:

Encounter chance per check = mode check × (1 − (1 − terrain chance of squad 1) × (1 − terrain chance of squad 2) × …)
(counting only moving squads on terrain with a monster)

Only squads that are moving, and on terrain where the mission lists a monster, count. For any other squad the game simply moves on to the next one. Every moving squad on good ground adds its own chance, in a mission or an Area Investigation, so more squads out on rough terrain means more encounters.

Talking a monster into joining

Talk uses one of the battle’s action points. Points build up over time during the battle, to a maximum of three, and the first arrives almost at once. A squad carrying a Charge Horn starts the battle with all three.

When you Talk, the game picks the first monster that is still standing and works out a persuasion score:

Score = leader affinity (30 to 80)
+ 50 × share of HP the monster has lost
(for some monsters: share of HP it still has)

Then it rolls from 0 to 99. If the roll is below the score, the monster joins your army. A score of 100 or more always succeeds.

If the monster says no, a second roll against its patience decides what happens next. Below its patience, the monster simply refuses (“was not persuaded”) and the battle carries on, with the monster striking back at once and getting back every attack it has already made. Otherwise the talk ends the battle, and nobody earns experience or items from it.

Most monsters listen more readily the more they are hurt. Pumpkinhead, Faerie, Gremlin, Golem, Stone Golem, and Baldr Golem work the other way: they are easiest to persuade at full health.

Leader affinity

Your squad leader’s class sets the first part of the score. Each kind of monster has one class that gets on with it best, worth 80, and a neighbouring class worth 60. The few monsters that can lead a squad, such as Vultans, Ravens, and Gorgons, count as their own kind. Princess and Vampire leaders are worth 60 with every monster. Any other leader is worth 30.

Named characters count as their class: Gilbert as Beast Master, Paul as Enchanter, Liedel as Archer, and Deneb as Witch. Biske is a good leader for beasts and Saradin for undead. Sheen scores 30 like an ordinary leader, and every other leader scores 30.

The Ogre that appears in Tybell has no persuasion entry at all. The game reads a blank entry for it, which gives a score far above 100, so Talk always recruits it. The same blank entry makes it run away the first time its turn comes up.

When its turn comes up, a monster whose HP is at or below its flee point runs away, ending the battle. Golems and Skeletons hold on until their HP is below 1% of their maximum.

Worked example

A squad led by a Dragon Tamer meets a Red Dragon in the highlands of Fair Heights. After a round of fighting, the dragon is down to 40% of its HP, which is above its 30% flee point.

StepValue
Leader affinity (Dragon Tamer and a dragon)60
HP lost: 60% × 5030
Score90
Chance it joins90%
If it refuses: patience 30%30% refuses and the battle goes on; 70% the talk ends the battle

A Knight leading the same squad would score 30 + 30 = 60. With a Dragon Master in charge the score would be 80 + 30 = 110, so the dragon would join every time.

Joining, fleeing, and rewards

A recruited monster joins your army at the level it had in the battle, taking the first free place in your roster.

If the monster flees, or the talk ends the battle, the encounter ends without it. Defeating the monster instead can earn an item, as with other enemies, and experience follows the usual rules; see Experience.

Tips

  • Put the right leader in front. A Dragon Master, Beast Master, or Enchanter turns the dragons, beasts, or golems of a mission into near-certain recruits.
  • Hurt it first, but not too much. For most monsters every tenth of their HP you take off adds 5 to the score. Stop before they reach their flee point.
  • Leave the gentle ones healthy. Faeries, Gremlins, Pumpkinheads, and Golems listen best before you hit them.
  • Patient monsters give second chances. Golems and Skeletons always just refuse, while a failed talk with a Faerie, Gremlin, Pumpkinhead, or Goblin usually ends the battle.
  • Hunt in Area Investigation. Once a mission is cleared, exploring its map finds monsters almost five times as often as the same squads would during the mission.
  • Send out every squad you can. Each moving squad on Forests, Highlands, or other good terrain adds its own chance, and an Area Investigation lets you deploy up to ten.
  • Wear a Decoy Cap to hunt. It doubles the terrain chance for the squad that has it equipped.
  • Farm monsters on rough ground. Highlands, forests, and the snowy terrains other than Snowy Plains produce encounters far more often than plains and roads.

Wild-monster glossary

Terrain chance

The chance, once the game’s first encounter check has passed, that a moving squad on that terrain meets a wild monster. A Decoy Cap in the squad doubles it.

Area Investigation

Exploring a mission’s map again after it has been cleared, from the world map. There is no enemy army, and wild monsters turn up far more often than during the mission.

Persuasion affinity

The base of the Talk chance, from 30 to 80, set by how well your squad leader’s class gets on with the monster’s kind.

Patience

The chance that a monster which turns down Talk simply refuses and the battle goes on. Otherwise the talk ends the battle, with no experience or items.

Flee point

The share of its maximum HP at or below which a wild monster runs away when its turn comes up, ending the battle.

Modder reference: Wild monsters and recruiting

Wild encounters run in three places: a scenario-overlay walk-step gate that picks the creature, a materializer that builds it at the scenario’s base level, and combat-overlay code that handles Talk, fleeing, and recruitment. The creature pools, terrain rates, persuasion ranks, and temperaments are all data. The Editor’s Encounters tab covers pools, rates, rewards, and custom squads.

Where these facts come from

Every location and value on this tab was read from the US retail ROM (revision 0 offsets, z64). Combat-overlay code runs at z64 + 0x7FFBCD30 and its actor helpers at z64 + 0x7FFBCB70. Monster levels were cross-checked against the wiki aide’s per-stage levels, all of which match. None of the suggested edits has been tried in a running game yet, so test each one from a cold boot before relying on it.

What do you want to change?

Change which monsters appear

Edit the pool slice for the scenario, or give a scenario its own slice through metadata byte 8.

See Creature pool and scenario selector · Walk-step encounter gate

Make a monster easier or harder to recruit

Edit its temperament row, or the ranks that decide affinity.

See Class behaviour resource · Talk persuasion · Persuasion affinity

Change how often encounters happen

Edit the terrain rates, or the global gate words. The Editor exposes both.

See Walk-step encounter gate

Change wild-monster levels

They follow the scenario base level (ESET byte 0x08), which also sets the enemy squads’ base.

See Wild-monster level

How to read the code and byte evidence

ROM offsets use big-endian z64 order. The master v64 stores each byte pair in reverse order. RAM addresses belong to the stated overlay or structure.

Each code line shows the z64 offset, the four original bytes, and the MIPS instruction. Relative branches name z64 destinations; J/JAL targets are encoded RAM addresses. The instruction after a branch is its delay slot.

Samples are stored bytes, not calculated values. For compressed resources, the sample gives the container’s ROM offset and the offset inside the decoded file.

Walk-step encounter gate

func_0013C060 runs while the scenario map updates. After several early gates it rolls rand() % 72000 against 10 (50 when state bit 17 of 0x80197168 is set; the comparison is ≤, so 11 or 51 passing values). It then tests up to 30 player units in a shuffled order (0x0013C230–0x0013C298): each resolves its terrain byte, rolls rand() % 100 against the terrain rate (doubled when the unit has item 242, Decoy Cap), and on success picks one byte of the slice’s pair with rand() % 2.

Retail terrain rates
Roads 10, Plains 15, Barrens 30, Forests 40, Marshes 30, Highlands 50, Snowy Plains 5, Snowy Barrens 35, Snowy Forests 45, Snowy Highlands 55; terrain bytes 0x00, 0x02, 0x08–0x0A, and 0x0F–0x1F have no slot.
Bit 17
Both visible writers in func_00102FA0 clear it; the setter has not been found, so the 51/72000 condition is still unnamed.
Staging
Class staged as 0x100 + class at 0x801F0E04, marker 46.
Overlay delta
The deployment hub runs at z64 + 0x8007FB70; the walk-step gate at z64 + 0x800AB8C0.
Moving squads
Candidates need unit flags & 0x60011 == 0x40011. Bit 0x40000 is set by func_0012D170 only while the unit is advancing along a route (cleared on every update, and on arrival), so stationary squads never roll.

How to change it

Raising a terrain byte’s rate to 50 or more makes a Decoy Cap guarantee the roll there; retail Highlands (50) and Snowy Highlands (55) already do.

Creature pool and scenario selector

Each slice holds ten two-byte pairs in terrain order (Roads, Plains, Barrens, Forests, Marshes, Highlands, then the four snowy terrains). A pair XX XX always gives class XX; AA BB picks one at random. A zero byte only fails the current unit: it is removed from the shuffled list and the remaining units are still tested (0x0013C41C–0x0013C464).

Slices in use
Pool data runs through slice 45 and ends at 0x00142257, just before the creature item table. Key 59 (Aurua Plains II) uses slice 41, key 63 slice 42, key 64 slice 43, and metadata rows 65 and 66 slices 44 and 45, all past the 40-slice framing of older notes; slices 40 (key 54) and 43 are empty. The code exits only for a value below 3; value 3 reads the all-zero slice 0 at 0x00141EC0.
Shared slices
Branch keys share slices, for example keys 15 and 16 (slice 14) and 40 and 55 (slice 31). Editing a slice changes every key that selects it.
Mission names
The ROM stores no names. The Companion joins keys to missions through the runtime-key labels and leaves out the low-confidence keys 58, 63, and 64.

Watch out for

  • Slices 41–45 overlap the bytes older tools treated as trailing padding. Don’t zero that area.

Wild-monster level

func_001960A8 copies ESET header byte 0x08 to 0x801F1035 (level 1 only when the ESET section-0 offset is 0, via beq $s2, $zero at 0x00196134), then to 0x80196AA4 and the shared neutral level 0x801936AC. The materializer func_0023B048 builds the creature at that level, adding 15 when 0x801936E0 is nonzero and the scenario key is 0x3F.

Cross-check
Every stage level in the wiki aide equals the ESET base level of its key, from Tenne Plains (2) to Aurua Plains II (36).
New game
func_00042800 and func_000428FC initialise the neutral level to 2.

Talk persuasion

func_0021495C returns 0 at once when byte 0x801936E0 is nonzero. Otherwise it takes the first of 20 actors that has flag 0x100 and none of bits 0–3, gets the affinity from func_00214750, and adds |b1 − HP / maxHP| × 50.0, where b1 is the target’s row byte 1. rand() % 100 < score returns 0 (joins). Otherwise rand() % 100 < b3 returns 2, and anything else returns 1.

Row byte 1
1 makes the term grow as HP falls; 0 makes it grow with HP left (Pumpkinhead, Faerie, Gremlin, and the golems).
Missing row
A class without a row reads the FF FF FF FF terminator, so b1 = 255 and the score always passes. Retail’s only such pool creature is Ogre (Tybell).
Talker
First actor with 0x100 clear and leader flag 0x200 set (func_0020C810). Affinity reads the talker’s and target’s word at +0x4C (the class byte at +0x4F); the temperament row uses +0x4B.

How to change it

Flip a monster’s preference by switching row byte 1 between 0 and 1. Set patience (byte 3) to 100 so a failed Talk never drives the squad off.

Watch out for

  • Adding a pool creature with no row makes Talk certain and makes it flee after the first round.

Persuasion affinity

Both classes are looked up in the rank table. With no talker the result is 0. A talker of rank 99 (Princess, Vampire) gives 60, equal ranks 80, ranks one apart 60, anything else 30. Classes absent from the table read rank 0xFF.

Retail ranks
Beasts 10 (Beast Master 10, Beast Tamer and Biske 11), golems 20 (Enchanter 20, Doll Master 21), dragons 30 (Dragon Master 30, Dragon Tamer 31), Faerie and Gremlin 40 (Archer, Diana 41), Pumpkinhead 50 (Witch 51), undead and Lich 60 (Archmage, Saradin 61), Vultan 70, Hawkman 71, Raven 72, Gorgon and Goblin 80; most human classes 0. Only classes with a nonzero leadership byte (class header name origin + 6) can be talkers, which rules out Hawkman, Goblin, and every beast, dragon, and golem.
Oddity
Two unlisted classes compare equal at 0xFF and score 80.

How to change it

To make a class a good leader for a kind, give it the kind’s rank (80) or rank ± 1 (60) in the pair table.

Class behaviour resource

Stored uncompressed: a size word (0x154) and a 340-byte buffer whose first two words are the offsets of the rank pairs (8) and the behaviour rows (0xC8). The Talk calculation and the flee test read the rows; the affinity helper reads the pairs.

Rows
34 rows [class, hurt-helps, flee %, patience %], for example Red Dragon 01 1E 1E, Golem 00 00 64, Faerie 00 32 0A.

Watch out for

  • Keep both terminators. Growing the buffer needs the size word and whatever follows at 0x008B1704 checked first.

Talk result states

State 0 of func_00219A14 calls the calculation and routes the result. Result 0 enters state 1, which shows “%s joined the battalion.” and calls the recruit at 0x00219D00; result 2 enters state 3 (“%s was not persuaded.”), sets owner byte +0x6074 (which makes func_00232280 move the monster to the front of the next attack schedule), and later requests phase 1; result 1 requests phase 11 from 0x00219EDC with no message; result 3 enters state 2.

Recruit
func_002142C4 copies the selected 52-byte scratch actor into the first free roster slot 1–99. With no free slot it falls back to slot 0 (0x00214314) and overwrites roster record 0 at 0x80193BC0; the visible effect is untested.
Phase 11
Also used by the terminal branch with +0x6088 nonzero; it returns without the results chain (no experience, graduation, or evolution).
Action budget
Combat owner word +0x1B0. The battle-start case of func_002152FC sets it to 0 with gauge +0x1AC = 259.0, or to 3 when the squad carries Charge Horn (0x1F, 0x00215380–0x002153A8). func_0021AE6C fills the gauge each pass and adds a point at 260, up to 3 (capped at 2 in training). Talk is menu slot 0 in a random-neutral battle (func_0020BF6C at 0x00215F60): it subtracts 1 (0x00215FB4) and requests phase 6 (func_00219A14, through the phase table at z64 0x00229D80). The 2-point slot-1 command (0x00216168) writes override 1, a loss; 0x00216458 is the squad-tactic change.

Flee threshold

func_00214BDC checks the random-neutral bit and the actor filters, then returns true when row byte 2 ≥ floor(HP × 100 / maxHP). The scheduler func_0022F2BC calls it when the actor comes up (0x0022F418); on true it exhausts every actor’s attacks and sets the neutral-retreat state, ending the battle mid-round.

Retail values
0 for Skeleton and the golems (flees only below 1% HP), 20 for the legendary dragons and Cerberus, 30 for most dragons and beasts, 50 for Ghost, Gorgon, Sphinx, Pumpkinhead, Faerie, and Gremlin.

CHARACTER & CAMPAIGN

Item drops

Which enemies carry items, how often they hand them over, and what every mission and wild monster can give you.

Most enemy squads carry one item, and a battle that the game counts gives you an 80% chance of receiving it. Each squad’s item can be won only once. The mission’s boss is different: its item is normally paid when you win the mission rather than in battle. Wild monsters give one of three items listed for their kind.

Where items come from

  • Enemy squads: 80% after a qualifying battle. Each squad carries at most one item, and your leader must still be standing for you to receive it.
  • The boss: paid at the end. The first squad of each mission, normally the boss, gives its item when the mission is won, with a few exceptions.
  • Wild monsters: one of three. Beating one gives a random item from its kind’s list.
  • Items don’t come back. Once a squad has dropped its item, it has nothing more to give in that mission.

Items carried by enemy squads

Each enemy squad in a mission is set up with at most one carried item. After a battle with that squad, the game rolls for it:

  • Your squad’s leader must still be alive and not turned to stone.
  • If so, the item drops 80% of the time and is added to your inventory.
  • If the roll fails, you don’t receive the item from that battle.
  • Once the item has dropped, that squad carries nothing more.

The drops recorded so far came from battles in which the enemy leader fell, so a failed roll usually means that item is gone for good. Exactly which battle results qualify isn’t known, and whether a battle that leaves the enemy leader standing can also produce the drop hasn’t been seen.

The mission-clear item

The first squad set up in each mission, normally the boss, holds the mission-clear item. It doesn’t drop in battle. Instead, the game gives it to you when you win the mission, with no roll, alongside the Goth and other end-of-mission rewards; see Scenario rewards.

Latium is the exception, because it has two bosses. While both are on the map, beating either one can drop its item in battle with the usual 80% chance. At the end of the mission the game pays the first boss’s item if it is still unclaimed, and otherwise the second boss’s. One version of Mount Keryoleth II skips the end-of-mission Goth and item altogether.

Wild monster items

Each kind of wild monster has a list of three items. When you beat one, the game picks one of the three at random and gives it to you, with no 80% roll. Your leader must again be alive and not turned to stone. See Wild monsters.

Other ways to get items

Items also come from sources this page doesn’t cover: hidden treasure on the mission maps, strongholds, story events, and shops.

Tips

  • Keep your leader safe. A squad whose leader has fallen or been petrified receives nothing, even if the rest of the squad wins.
  • One item per squad. Once a squad’s item has dropped, beating it again gives nothing more.
  • Hunt rare monsters for rare items. Legendary dragons, Cerberus, and Sphinx carry Goblets of Destiny, Angel Fruit, and other rare items.
  • The boss’s item comes at the end. Apart from Latium, you receive it by winning the mission, not by beating the boss in battle.

Item-drop glossary

Carried item

The one item an enemy squad can drop, fixed for that squad in that mission. Once it has been dropped, the squad no longer has it.

Mission-clear item

The item carried by a mission’s first squad, normally its boss. Except on Latium, it never drops in battle; you normally receive it when the mission is won.

Creature item list

Three items listed for each kind of wild monster. Defeating one gives you one of the three at random.

Modder reference: Item drops

Squad items are data in each mission’s ESET resource, copied into a runtime slot table when the mission loads. After a battle, the mission state machine rolls for the opponent’s slot; the boss slot is instead paid out by mission settlement. Wild monsters use a separate class-indexed table. The Editor’s Scenario tab edits deployment items and its Encounters tab edits creature items.

Where these facts come from

ROM locations and values on this tab were read from the US retail ROM (z64); RAM addresses and the savestate facts come from runtime observation. The per-mission item lists come from the Editor’s byte-exact ESET census, and 515 of the wiki’s 530 listed squad drops appear in them. Mission-clear items match the wiki’s boss reward for 41 of 43 missions; Mount Keryoleth II (no wiki reward) and Aurua Plains II (the wiki credits the named bosses, which are ordinary sources 0x1F–0x22) differ. None of the suggested edits has been tried in a running game yet, so test each one from a cold boot before relying on it.

Where the data lives

DataLocationFormatIn the Editor
Squad itemsESET Section 1 row bytes 10–12Byte 10 = equipment flag, bytes 11–12 = item IDScenario tab
Runtime slotsRAM 0x8019367C + 2 × source (source ≥ 0x1E)u16, bit 15 = equipment, 0 = empty—
Creature itemsz64 0x001422588-byte records [0, class, 3 × u16]Encounters tab

The creature table lies outside the CRC-checked region. ESET resources are compressed archives; export them through the Editor.

Award conditions

SourceConditionsChance
Ordinary squadResult 1 with byte 0x80193670 nonzero, post-battle routine returns 0, source ≠ 0x1E, player leader alive and not petrified, opponent object bit 0x10 clear, slot nonzero80%, or certain for keys 0x3F–0x42
Boss (source 0x1E)Mission settlement: returns early when event predicate 17 is set or the staged key is 0x3F; key 0x36 (a Mount Keryoleth II alias) skips Goth and itemCertain
Wild monsterRandom-neutral flag, byte 0x80193670 bit 0x10, player leader alive and not petrifiedCertain; slot by rand() % 3 (lookup value read statically from 0x801976E8)

Keys 0x2D/0x2E (Latium) branch at 0x001025E0: source 0x1E can be paid in battle while the 0x1F object (*0x801F0D2C) has flags & 0x11, and source 0x1F while the 0x1E object (*0x801F0D28) does; the 80% roll at 0x001026C8 follows, the player-leader checks are skipped for those two sources, and settlement then falls back to slot 1 if slot 0 was paid.

What do you want to change?

Change what a squad carries

Edit its ESET Section 1 row bytes 10–12 in the Scenario tab.

See Deployment item source

Change the drop chance

Edit the slti …, 0x50 compare in the award path.

See After-battle drop award

Change wild-monster items

Edit the class’s three slots in the creature table.

See Creature item table

Change the mission-clear item

Edit the item of the mission’s source 0x1E row.

See Mission-clear item · Deployment item source

How to read the code and byte evidence

ROM offsets use big-endian z64 order. The master v64 stores each byte pair in reverse order. RAM addresses belong to the stated overlay or structure.

Each code line shows the z64 offset, the four original bytes, and the MIPS instruction. Relative branches name z64 destinations; J/JAL targets are encoded RAM addresses. The instruction after a branch is its delay slot.

Samples are stored bytes, not calculated values. For compressed resources, the sample gives the container’s ROM offset and the offset inside the decoded file.

After-battle drop awardCreature item tableDeployment item sourceMission-clear itemLeader checks

After-battle drop award

func_00101DDC runs when the mission map resumes. With result 0x80186FF0 = 1 it rewrites the result to 3 when byte 0x80193670 is 0; otherwise it calls func_00119454, and a zero return reaches the award block. The block reads the opponent’s slot, then branches: wild monsters (flag 0x40 at 0x801976D8) look up the creature table, and all other squads go through the leader checks and the 80% roll.

Roll
rand() % 100 (magic 0x51EB851F), slti $v0, $v0, 0x50 at 0x001027DC.
Boss exclusion
beq $s4, $s0 with $s0 = 0x1E at 0x00102780.
After an award
The item goes to the reward queue and the slot is cleared (sh $zero, 0x367C(…) at 0x001028BC).
Savestate check
In the vanilla Tenne pair, the battle with source 33 ends with its leader at 0 HP and the slot’s Ninja’s Garb (0x809D) moves to the queue at 0x801F0B50.

How to change it

Change 0x50 at 0x001027DC (28420050) to 0x64 for certain drops, or lower it for rarer ones. The Latium path has its own compare at 0x001026C8.

Watch out for

  • The award block never tests whether the enemy leader died. What byte 0x80193670 and func_00119454 contribute is not decoded, so don’t assume every battle qualifies. In the vanilla Tenne states, source 0x22 ends with its leader at 0 HP and its Iron Claw still in slot 4: a failed roll, with no evidence the squad can be fought again.

Creature item table

35 active records keyed by class, followed by a zero sentinel. The award scans for the opponent class, takes rand() % 3, and uses that slot; a zero slot gives nothing.

Lookup
0x0010245C–0x001024D0; the scan compares the record’s first halfword (0 and class) with the byte at 0x801976E8. That byte holds the class before combat and a transient source ID during it; its value when the award runs has not been observed, so this is a static reading.
Reward flag
The wild path also requires bit 0x10 of byte 0x80193670.

How to change it

Repeat an item across slots to make it more likely. The Editor’s weighted rewards replace the three-way roll with custom weights.

func_001390F0 takes slot 0 or, when it is 0, slot 1, awards it through func_00130E60 after the Goth reward, and clears slot 0. Slot 0 is nonzero in every retail key, but the Latium path can clear it before settlement, so the fallback is live there.
