CHARACTER & CAMPAIGN

Items you use and carry

What every usable item does, exactly how much it gives, and which items a squad can carry for a lasting effect.

Items fall into three groups. Recovery items heal HP, remove fatigue, or undo petrification and death. Rare treasures permanently change an attribute, Alignment, Luck, or level by a small random amount. Carried items sit in a squad’s carrying slots and quietly help it for as long as they stay there.

How items work

  • Some items help one character, others a whole squad. Heal Leaf treats one character; Heal Pack treats everyone in the squad.
  • Healing can’t raise the fallen. Only an Altar of Resurrection brings a fallen character back.
  • Boost items are random, within a range. A Sword Emblem adds 2 to 4 STR, for example.
  • Carried items work while carried. A squad has up to ten carrying slots, depending on its members’ classes.

Healing and recovery

ItemUsed onEffectPrice
Heal LeafOne character+100 HP (not a fallen character)10 Goth
Heal SeedOne character+300 HP (not a fallen character)50 Goth
Heal PackEvery member of a squad+150 HP each (fallen members aren’t healed)120 Goth
Power FruitEvery member of a squad−20 fatigue each80 Goth
Angel FruitEvery member of a squad−50 fatigue each200 Goth
Revive StoneOne characterCures petrification500 Goth
Altar of ResurrectionOne characterRestores HP to full, bringing a fallen character back, and cures petrificationNot sold

Healing never goes above maximum HP, and fatigue never drops below zero. See Fatigue for what fatigue does in battle and Petrification for what a Revive Stone cures.

Permanent boosts

These treasures make a permanent change to one character. The amount is rolled when the item is used.

ItemEffect
Champion Statuette+1 level, with the usual growth for that level (nothing at level 99); see Attribute growth
Cup of Life+5 to +10 maximum HP (current HP unchanged)
Sword Emblem+2 to +4 STR
Bracer of Protection+2 to +4 VIT
Crown of Intellect+2 to +4 INT
Mirror of Soul+2 to +4 MEN
Stone of Quickness+2 to +4 AGI
Crystal of Precision+2 to +4 DEX
Scroll of Discipline+1 to +3 Alignment
Urn of Chaos−1 to −3 Alignment
Goblet of Destiny−1, 0, or +1 Luck

Attributes stop at 999; Alignment and Luck stay between 0 and 100.

See Alignment for what the Scroll and Urn change. Flag of Unity works on a squad instead: it raises the squad’s Unity by 1 to 5, up to 100; see Unity.

Items a squad carries

A squad has up to ten slots for carried items, depending on its members’ classes. The items below work for as long as the squad carries them.

ItemWhile the squad carries it
Manual of WarfareDoubles the experience its members earn; see Experience
Medal of VigorDoubles the leader’s Soldier-graduation progress; see Soldier graduation
Ansate CrossA graduating Soldier becomes an Amazon instead of a Fighter, or the reverse
Mastaba’s BarrierProtects fallen members from becoming Zombies after a scenario; see Automatic class changes
Charge HornStarts every battle with all three action points instead of building them up; see Wild monsters
Figurine of SleipnirThe squad moves twice as fast on the map
Marching BatonBy day, marching tires the squad at a half to a third of the usual rate
Censer of ReposeBy day, resting recovers the squad twice as fast

Marching, resting, and fatigue

Squads tire as they march. Every so often each standing, unpetrified member gains 1 fatigue, up to 100, and this happens faster at night. While a squad rests, for example in a stronghold you hold, the opposite happens: at each recovery step each standing, unpetrified member loses 2 fatigue and regains 1 HP, and night speeds this up too.

A Marching Baton cuts how fast marching builds toward the next point of fatigue to a half, or a third in some situations, and a Censer of Repose doubles how fast resting reaches the next recovery step. The night-time speed-up is added on top and isn’t changed by either item.

Story and special items

Letters, packages, the Pedras, and similar items belong to the story and can’t be used from the item menu. The effects of Quit Gate (sold in every shop for 150 Goth), Silver Hourglass, Dowsing Rod, and Love and Peace aren’t known yet.

Tips

  • Use Heal Pack for spread-out damage. It gives 150 HP to every standing member, so with three or more hurt members it heals more in total than a Heal Seed.
  • Keep Angel Fruit for long marches. It clears 50 fatigue from the whole squad, which always brings every member below the fatigue-penalty range.
  • Mind the limits. Alignment and Luck stop at 0 and 100, so a Scroll of Discipline used at Alignment 100 is wasted.
  • Give squads a job-specific kit. A Figurine of Sleipnir for a fast raiding squad, a Manual of Warfare for one being trained up, and a Censer of Repose for one guarding a stronghold.
  • Carry a Charge Horn when hunting wild monsters. Starting with three action points lets you Talk at once.

Item glossary

Squad item

An item that works on every member of the chosen squad at once, such as Heal Pack or Power Fruit.

Carried item

An item placed in one of a squad’s carrying slots. Carried items with a lasting effect aren’t used up; they work for as long as the squad carries them.

Fatigue

A character’s tiredness from 0 to 100. From 70 upward it weakens attack, defense, accuracy, and evasion in battle.

Modder reference: Items you use and carry

Menu-used consumables go through one resident dispatcher that first rolls an amount and then applies it. The consumable table decides whether an item targets one character or a whole squad. Carried items are plain bytes in each squad record, tested by a battle helper and a map helper wherever an effect applies.

Where these facts come from

Every location and value on this tab was read from the US retail ROM (z64). Resident code runs at z64 + 0x8012A100, Army-overlay code at + 0x801135A0, scenario-overlay code at + 0x800AB8C0, the main combat overlay at + 0x7FFBCD30, and combat helpers at + 0x7FFBCB70. None of the suggested edits has been tried in a running game yet, so test each one from a cold boot before relying on it.

What do you want to change?

Change how much an item heals or boosts

Edit the constant in the dispatcher case.

See Item-effect dispatcher

Make an item work on the whole squad

Set its target byte to 2. The menu rolls each member’s amount with the selected character as the target, so a squad-wide Altar would heal everyone by the selected character’s max HP.

See Consumable records · Army-menu item use

Change a carried item’s effect

Find its test through the battle or map carried-item helper.

See Map carried-item test · Charge Horn · Resting timer · Marching timer

How to read the code and byte evidence

ROM offsets use big-endian z64 order. The master v64 stores each byte pair in reverse order. RAM addresses belong to the stated overlay or structure.

Each code line shows the z64 offset, the four original bytes, and the MIPS instruction. Relative branches name z64 destinations; J/JAL targets are encoded RAM addresses. The instruction after a branch is its delay slot.

Samples are stored bytes, not calculated values. For compressed resources, the sample gives the container’s ROM offset and the offset inside the decoded file.

Item-effect dispatcherConsumable recordsArmy-menu item useCharge HornMap carried-item testResting timerMarching timerFigurine of Sleipnir

Item-effect dispatcher

func_00041098(mode, amount, item, target) bounds-checks item − 1 < 19 and jumps through the table. With mode 0 each case returns its rolled amount; with mode 1 it applies amount to the roster record 0x80193BC0 + 56 × target. Targets of 100 and above use the special-pool arrays (current HP 0x80190EBC + 2 × id, one maximum at 0x80190F82, status 0x80191010 + id), which the map rest step also uses; the heal there works in thirds of the maximum.

Cases
Heal Leaf and Seed share 0x000410EC; Heal Pack 0x00041108; Power and Angel Fruit 0x0004123C; Revive Stone 0x00041288 (clears status bit 0x04); Altar 0x000412CC (heal by max HP, clear 0x04); Quit Gate returns 0; Champion Statuette 0x00041308; Cup of Life 0x00041334; attribute items 0x000413CC–0x00041428; Scroll 0x00041484; Urn 0x00041500; Goblet 0x00041558.
Heal guard
The ordinary heal shared by Heal Leaf, Heal Seed, and Heal Pack (0x0004120C) does nothing when current HP is 0, so only the Altar revives.
Caps
Heals stop at the character’s max HP (+0x16); max HP and attributes stop at 999; Alignment and Luck at 0–100. The Statuette does nothing at level 99 (sltiu …, 0x63 at 0x00044ADC).

How to change it

Removing the zero-HP guard at 0x00041214 would let Heal Leaf, Heal Seed, and Heal Pack all revive; the Altar case already heals without it.

Army-menu item use

After choosing an item, the handler asks func_00045440 for its target. A target of 1 rolls once and applies to the chosen character; otherwise it walks the squad’s nine member slots (+0x1180, 0xFF = empty), rolling and applying per member. Flag of Unity is special-cased by ID.

Flag of Unity
+0x119B of the squad’s active record gains the rolled 1–5, capped at 100 (0x000CA38C–0x000CA3A4).

Charge Horn

Battles normally start with 0 action points and a gauge of 259.0 that reaches 260 almost at once. A carried Charge Horn stores 3 points instead. Points gate the wild-encounter Fight and Talk commands and the squad-tactic change. This code is in the main combat overlay (the 260.0 threshold is at z64 0x00229A98).

Map carried-item test

func_00131480 checks the ten carried bytes of the unit’s squad. Its four callers are the Sleipnir double update, the Censer rest rate, the Baton march rate, and the Mastaba’s Barrier death-change mask.

Also carried
The same ten bytes hold ordinary consumables; enemy squads start with Revive Stones there. Usable capacity depends on the members’ class byte B59.

Resting timer

When func_00133700 decides a unit is resting (flag 0x20000, an inactive unit with bit 0x1 clear, or one stationed at a site with flag 0x4, or flag 0x2 for player units), it lowers the unit’s +0xB6 timer by 3, or 6 with Censer of Repose, and by 2 more at night. Each time the timer wraps it resets to 180 and func_00133BE0 gives every standing, unpetrified member of the five member slots −2 fatigue and +1 HP. Rest is only checked when the march check returns −1 (func_00133234, 0x00133434–0x00133454).

Timer
Unit object +0xB6, u16; 180 per step. Hour byte 0x801F0E0A; hours 6–17 count as day.

Watch out for

  • The exact resting conditions (site flags at 0x801951B0 + 36 × site + 0x1C, func_00131984) are not fully named.

CHARACTER & CAMPAIGN

How equipment works

Which items each class can use, which pieces are locked in place, and what equipment really adds in battle.

Every class has up to four equipment slots, and each slot takes one kind of item: the kind of the class’s own standard piece for that slot. A Knight’s weapon slot takes one-handed swords and nothing else, for example. You also need an unused copy, and a few special pieces can never be chosen at all. A slot with nothing chosen uses the standard piece, so no usable slot is ever empty.

Equipment at a glance

  • The class sets the slots. A class’s standard pieces decide how many slots it has and what type each accepts.
  • Types must match exactly. A one-handed sword slot won’t take a two-handed sword or a rapier, and a helm slot won’t take headgear.
  • You need a spare. Choosing an item uses an unused copy from your inventory, except for the class’s standard piece, which is always available.
  • Some pieces are fixed. A few classes can never change certain slots.
  • Equipment feeds the battle formulas. Its bonuses count in attack, defense, accuracy, evasion, resistance, and the Luck comparisons of the hit and damage checks.

Slots by class

The first slot holds the weapon and the second the body armour. The third holds a shield, a spellbook, or an accessory, and the fourth a helm, headgear, or an accessory, depending on the class. A dash means the class has no item there, so the slot can’t be used.

Only the generic classes are listed. Story classes such as Magnus’s Gladiator line also have slots; dragons, beasts, golems, and similar monsters have none.

Some pieces exist only as a class’s standard or fixed equipment and can never be chosen from the equip menu, even though they show in the list: Knoevlfer, Sonic Blade, Clau Solace, Short Spear, Hemlock, Scepter, Half Armor, Breast Leather, Elem Plate, Tiny Clothing, Count’s Garment, Quilted Cloth, Royal Garb, Cross Helm, Jelton Helm, Glass Pumpkin, Dream Tiara, Royal Crown, Bloody Emblem, Ring of the Dead, Fur-lined Mantle, Majestic Mantle, Blue Sash, Tunic, and Guard Tunic.

Choosing an item

The equip menu lists every item of the slot’s type that you own, but it only lets you pick one that has an unused copy. The class’s standard piece is the exception: its copy is set aside for the character, so choosing it always works and simply returns the slot to its standard piece. Switching away from the standard piece doesn’t release that set-aside copy.

Magnus’s own classes and some other story classes have fixed pieces too.

What equipment adds

Item valueWhat it does
STR on the first weaponAdded to the Physical Attack Coefficient in physical attack power, and to STR in physical defense
STR on other itemsAdded to STR in physical attack power and physical defense (a second weapon’s STR counts only in defense)
VIT, INT, MEN, AGI, DEXAdded where the damage and accuracy formulas show an equipment bonus; equipment INT joins the Magic Attack Coefficient in magic attack power, and equipment DEX joins the coefficient in the alternate physical power some classes use
ResistancesAdded to the class’s resistance to that element
Luck modifierAdded to Luck in the hit check and the damage Luck difference, but not in the double-damage check; it doesn’t change the character’s own Luck
ElementThe first spellbook sets the element of the caster’s ordinary spells (a plain Spellbook uses the caster’s own element); without one, the first weapon supplies it if it has an element, and otherwise the caster’s own element is used. The weapon’s element also changes magic power depending on the spell’s element
Growth (30 items only)Most equipment has none. Thirty rare items, such as Firecrest, Stone Sword, and Saint’s Shield, add points to certain attributes at each level-up while worn, and those points stay
Anti-dragon (attack)+5 to attack conditions against dragons: Fafnir, Sword of Firedrake, Sword of Tiamat, Balmung, Gram, Axe of Wyrm, and Cyanic Claw
Anti-dragon (defense)+5 to defense conditions against dragons: Dragon Shield, Dragon Armor, Dragon Helm, and Fang of Firedrake

See Attack power and defense and Accuracy and evasion for where each bonus enters, Resistance for elements, Which spell each caster uses for spell elements, and Attribute growth for growth equipment. Casting without any weapon triggers a known bug in magic power; see Special attacks and other rules. A shield of either kind protects against Gaze of Terror; see Petrification.

Changing class and equipment

Changing class removes everything the character was wearing and equips the new class’s standard pieces, buying any that are needed; see Changing class. Because the new class may take different types, gear that suited the old class may not fit at all.

Tips

  • Check the type before you buy. A shop sword is useless to a Fencer if it is one-handed, because Fencers use two-handed swords.
  • A spellbook decides a caster’s element. Swap books to change a Wizard’s spells without changing class.
  • Keep a spare for rare fixed pieces. A new Princess needs an unused Battle Fan and Dream Tiara, which can’t be bought when changing class.

Equipment glossary

Equipment type

The kind of item, such as 1H Sword, Heavy Shield, or Headgear. A slot offers only items of exactly the type of the class’s standard piece for that slot.

Standard piece

The item a class uses in a slot when nothing else has been chosen. It sets which equipment type the slot accepts.

Fixed slot

A slot whose standard piece can’t be swapped out, such as the Princess’s Dream Tiara.

Modder reference: How equipment works

Equipment permission is not a separate table: each class slot accepts exactly the item type of the class’s standard piece in that slot, and B42 locks individual slots. Item records carry the bonuses; the combat formulas in the Damage and Accuracy tabs show where each enters.

Where these facts come from

Every location and value on this tab was read from the US retail ROM (z64). Resident code runs at z64 + 0x8012A100 and Army-overlay code at z64 + 0x801135A0. None of the suggested edits has been tried in a running game yet, so test each one from a cold boot before relying on it.

How to read the code and byte evidence

ROM offsets use big-endian z64 order. The master v64 stores each byte pair in reverse order. RAM addresses belong to the stated overlay or structure.

Each code line shows the z64 offset, the four original bytes, and the MIPS instruction. Relative branches name z64 destinations; J/JAL targets are encoded RAM addresses. The instruction after a branch is its delay slot.

Samples are stored bytes, not calculated values. For compressed resources, the sample gives the container’s ROM offset and the offset inside the decoded file.

Effective item per slotEquip-slot candidate listFixed-slot maskWeapon and spellbook tests

Effective item per slot

Every slot resolves to the character’s override or, when the override is 0, the class standard item. A slot whose standard item is 0 can’t be used: the menu’s zero test at 0x000D1C64–0x000D1C68 (repeated at 0x000D1F50) refuses it with message 0x4000C, and func_000D1564 skips the candidate list, writing a count of 1.

Selectors
Four functions through 0x801EF288, called with the primary and secondary class; they read the class record’s standard items (B34/B36/B38/B40, honouring the B57 mapping).

Equip-slot candidate list

The list is every inventory entry (0x80196B00 + 4 × index, 0x116 entries) with a nonzero owned count and the same type byte as the slot’s effective item; it ignores the in-use count. Confirming a choice then applies two more checks: item byte +2 must be nonzero (func_00045514 at 0x000D1F5C, message 0x40062), and unless the choice is the standard piece, in-use must be below owned (0x000D1FFC–0x000D2014). Choosing the standard piece writes override 0.

Exact match
bnel $v0, $s4 at 0x000BC798: 1H Sword, 2H Sword, and Rapier are different types, as are Helm and Headgear.
Menu-locked items
25 retail items have byte +2 = 0, including Dream Tiara, Ring of the Dead, Bloody Emblem, Count’s Garment, Blue Sash, Short Spear, and Half Armor: they appear only as standard or fixed pieces.

Watch out for

  • Changing a class’s standard piece to another type also changes which items every member of that class can wear, and leaves existing overrides of the old type in place until the next class change.
  • The standard piece’s copy is reserved at class change and not released when the player switches away from it; the menu adjusts in-use only for non-standard items (0x000D2030, 0x000D2080).
  • Changing a class’s standard item in a ROM breaks the reserved-copy counts of characters already in that class: the next class change subtracts an in-use count from the new standard item (0x000CEF08–0x000CEF54) without checking for 0x1FF, which can underflow or write outside the inventory table.

Weapon and spellbook tests

Combat takes the weapon STR bonus and weapon element from the first item, in slot order, that passes the weapon test, and the spell element from the first spellbook, which takes priority.

CHARACTER & CAMPAIGN

Squads, Legions, and enemy groups

How many characters fit in a squad, how a squad’s movement is decided, and how Legions and enemy groups travel together.

A squad holds up to five characters on a three-by-three formation grid, with large monsters counting double. It crosses the map using the most restrictive movement type among its members, and up to five squads can travel together as a group. Enemy squads use the same group system, and some of them wait in place until the mission wakes them.

Squads at a glance

  • Five places per squad. A large monster counts as two, and nobody can stand next to one.
  • One member’s type decides. The squad moves as whichever member’s movement type comes first in a fixed order, so a single Plain-type character keeps a squad of fliers on the ground.
  • Legions travel together. A leading squad and up to four others move as one group.
  • Enemies group up too. Enemy squads move in formation around a lead squad, and some lie dormant until triggered.

Building a squad

Each character stands on one square of the three-by-three formation grid, in the front, middle, or back row; the row decides their attacks, see Attacks by row. A squad has five places:

Full squads

Squad make-upPlaces used
Five regular characters5
Three regular characters and one large one5
One regular character and two large ones5

A large character counts as two places, and no other character may stand on any of the eight squares around it, diagonals included. The large classes are Ogre, Young Dragon, Thunder Dragon, Red Dragon, Earth Dragon, Blue Dragon, Platinum Dragon, Black Dragon, Quetzalcoatl, Flarebrass, Ahzi Dahaka, Hydra, Bahamut, Tiamat, Wyrm, Wyvern, Griffin, Opinincus, Cockatrice, Sphinx, Hellhound, Cerberus, Golem, Stone Golem, and Baldr Golem.

Movement types

Every class has a movement type. A squad uses the first type in this list that any of its members has. The order is fixed; it doesn’t compare speeds on the terrain at hand, so a squad with a Marsh member and a Forest member always moves as Marsh:

Movement types of the regular classes, in priority order

OrderMovement typeClasses
1ImmobileVampire (in coffin) and Giant
2PlainSoldier, Fighter, Lycanthrope, Knight, Berserker, Fencer, Phalanx, Doll Master, Wizard, Dragon Tamer, Witch, Sorceress, Cleric, Paladin, Dragoon, Black Knight, Sword Master, Cataphract, Enchanter, Archmage, Dragon Master, Siren, Priest, Princess, Centurion (Male), Centurion (Female), Lich, Vampire, Skeleton, Gorgon, Goblin, Ogre, Young Dragon, Thunder Dragon, Earth Dragon, Black Dragon, Quetzalcoatl, Ahzi Dahaka, and Tiamat
3MarshZombie (Male), Zombie (Female), Blue Dragon, and Hydra
4ForestAmazon, Ninja, Archer, Ninja Master, Diana, Pumpkinhead, and Saturos
5SnowValkyrie, Freya, Platinum Dragon, and Bahamut
6MountainBeast Tamer, Beast Master, Werewolf, Red Dragon, Flarebrass, Hellhound, Cerberus, Golem, Stone Golem, and Baldr Golem
7SkyAngel Knight, Seraph, Hawkman, Vultan, Raven, Ghost, Faerie, Gremlin, Wyrm, Wyvern, Griffin, Opinincus, Cockatrice, and Sphinx

A squad whose members are all fliers moves as Sky; adding one Knight makes it move as Plain. The same rule decides how a group of squads moves.

Story characters’ own classes move as Plain, with three exceptions: Leia’s Blaze Knight and Rune Knight move as Snow, and Gilbert’s Beast Master moves as Mountain. Biske moves as Plain in both forms, unlike an ordinary Werewolf.

Only the Vampire’s daytime coffin form and the Giant have the Immobile type among regular classes. By day a Vampire sleeps in its coffin, so any squad with a Vampire can’t move until night. Other Immobile squads you meet are special story units, such as Danika’s forms.

Legions

You can join up to five of your squads into a Legion. The Legion travels as one group, with its other squads keeping formation around its first squad, the leader. It uses the same movement-type order across all its squads.

Soldiers in the Legion’s first squad never gain graduation progress, however well that squad fights. Put Soldiers you want to graduate into the Legion’s other squads, or into squads outside a Legion; see Soldier graduation.

Enemy groups

Enemy squads use the same group system: a lead squad and up to four others travel together, the others keeping a formation around the lead.

  • **Some enemy squads start dormant.** They sit still until the mission wakes their group, for example when one of your squads enters a particular area. Not every camp is woken the same way.
  • Some enemy squads hunt. When their current orders allow it, they head for the nearest of your squads within a short distance.
  • Groups use the same movement-type order as your own squads, so one member’s type decides for the whole group.

Tips

  • Keep flying squads pure. One ground-bound member makes the whole squad move as its type.
  • Choose your Legion leader carefully. Its Soldiers never graduate, so lead with a squad that has none.
  • Plan around large monsters. Two dragons leave room for only one other character.
  • Expect ambushes. Dormant groups can wake when your squads reach certain areas, so a quiet camp may not stay quiet.

Squad glossary

Large character

A dragon, beast, golem, or similar monster that counts as two of a squad’s five places and keeps every neighbouring square of the formation empty.

Movement type

How a class crosses the map: Sky, Plain, Forest, Mountain, Snow, Marsh, or Immobile. A squad, and a group of squads, uses whichever of its members’ types comes first in a fixed priority order.

Legion

A group of up to five of your squads, including the first squad that leads it, that travels together.

Dormant squad

An enemy squad that waits in place until something in the mission wakes it.

Modder reference: Squads, Legions, and enemy groups

Squads, enemy groups, and Legions share one movement-type reducer. Groups and Legions also share one ten-record descriptor table; each squad’s own type lives in its squad record. Enemy groups, dormancy, and aggro are documented in detail in the enemy movement notes; this tab collects what a modder needs to change them.

Where these facts come from

Locations and values were read from the US retail ROM (z64). Resident code runs at z64 + 0x8012A100, Army-overlay code at z64 + 0x801135A0, scenario-overlay code at z64 + 0x800AB8C0, and overlay descriptor 17 (z64 0x69900) at z64 + 0x8012E270. The enemy movement facts are from the reviewed enemy-movement research. None of the suggested edits has been tried in a running game yet, so test each one from a cold boot before relying on it.

How to read the code and byte evidence

ROM offsets use big-endian z64 order. The master v64 stores each byte pair in reverse order. RAM addresses belong to the stated overlay or structure.

Each code line shows the z64 offset, the four original bytes, and the MIPS instruction. Relative branches name z64 destinations; J/JAL targets are encoded RAM addresses. The instruction after a branch is its delay slot.

Samples are stored bytes, not calculated values. For compressed resources, the sample gives the container’s ROM offset and the offset inside the decoded file.

Movement-type priorityGroup descriptorsSquad size rules

Movement-type priority

The reducer copies its five arguments to the stack and scans the priority table outermost, so the earliest-listed type present wins; it compares no speeds or terrain. Immobile is both first in the table and the no-match fallback. Only the coffin Vampire (0x2C) and the Giant carry it among regular classes; whether the coffin class reaches map movement, and what type 7 does on the map, hasn’t been checked.

Callers
Army overlay func_000BD154, func_000BD26C, func_000C0EDC; overlay descriptor 17 func_0006D7D8 (writes the player squad record’s byte 24, the squad movement type) and func_0006D96C; scenario overlay func_00129068, func_001291B4, func_00129268, func_0012A574, func_0012A958; and func_002487E0 (segment not labelled). A whole-ROM scan finds these eleven jal 0x8016B088 sites and no others.
Unique classes
Story classes 0x51–0x60 are Plain except Blaze Knight and Rune Knight (Snow) and Beast Master (Mountain); Biske’s Werewolf (0x60) is Plain.

Group descriptors

The same ten records carry enemy groups and player Legions. Bytes 2–6 hold five squad IDs including the anchor, so a group is the anchor plus up to four followers. Byte 9 is the aggregate movement type from the priority reducer; byte 8 selects the formation pattern whose vector table places followers around the anchor.

Legion rule
The Soldier-graduation gain (func_002152FC, 0x2157D8–0x2157E4) skips the first unit of a matching in-use record, so a Legion’s lead squad never earns progress. The Army writer also sets flag 0x02 on that squad’s record.
Shared pool
func_000C1D68 (0xC2018–0xC208C) claims a record whose bit 0 is clear; func_001D207C clears all 0x6E bytes at init. The Army side keeps 10 Legion records (14 bytes at army base +0x10D4), but its reuse check scans only 6.
Enemy behaviour
Dormant groups (kind-2 start node), wake requests, formation projection, and proximity aggro ((1.8 × scale)²) are in the enemy movement notes.

Watch out for

  • Enemy groups and Legions draw from one ten-record pool by construction; whether a mission ever exhausts it hasn’t been checked.

Squad size rules

Regular members cost one of five places and large members two; a large member also blocks its eight neighbours. Code tests only size == 2. The Editor’s squad builder enforces the same rule.

CHARACTER & CAMPAIGN

Chaos Frame

The hidden reputation that decides who joins you, which ending you see, and part of your Goth: what moves it, and by how much.

Chaos Frame is your army’s reputation with the people, a hidden number from 0 to 100 that starts at 50. It rises when your squads liberate strongholds and falls when they capture them or lose them back to the enemy. Many story scenes and dialogue choices move it too, by 5 to 20 at a time. It decides whether some characters will join you, which ending you see, and part of each scenario’s Goth reward.

Chaos Frame at a glance

  • Match the squad to the town. Taking a stronghold compares the squad’s average Alignment with the town’s Morale. Close means up to +2; far means as much as −5.
  • Hold what you take. Each time an enemy squad retakes one of your strongholds, Chaos Frame drops by 2.
  • It is kept hidden until the end. The game shows the number only after the ending credits; while you play, the clearest signs are the messages when you take enemy towns and who offers to join.
  • Story choices matter most. A single answer in a story scene can move it by 10 or 20, far more than any one town.
  • It stays between 0 and 100. Changes past either end are lost.

Liberating and capturing strongholds

When one of your squads takes a stronghold, the game compares the squad’s average Alignment, counting every member at their current Alignment (Soldiers included), with the town’s Morale:

Score = difference between squad average and town Morale
+ town penalty (0 or 40)
+ random 0–7

Taking a stronghold

ScoreChaos FrameMessage at an enemy town
0–5+2Liberated
6–15+1Liberated
16–300Liberated
31–50−1Captured
51–80−2Captured
81–110−3Captured
111–140−4Captured
141 or more−5Captured

At a town the enemy holds, the message tells you which side of the line you landed on: “liberated” means the score was 30 or less, “captured” means it was 31 or more, and a score of 16–30 is a liberation that leaves Chaos Frame unchanged. Neutral towns always report “captured”, even when Chaos Frame goes up, so don’t judge a neutral town by its message. The random part is small, so a squad well inside a band always gets the same result.

  • Some towns never change it. Most missions’ enemy headquarters, and a few other sites such as Volmus Mine while it is neutral and Dardunnelles, leave Chaos Frame alone whoever takes them. They are marked “no change” in the table below.
  • **A few towns carry a hidden penalty.** 40 points are added to their score, so even a perfectly matched squad scores at least 40 and loses Chaos Frame there. They are marked † in the table below.
  • Only your own squads count. Enemy squads taking towns use a separate rule; see below.

What Chaos Frame decides

Recruits. These characters check Chaos Frame before they offer to join:

CharacterMissionChaos FrameAlso needs
Liedel (Archer)#1334 or moreAt the end of the mission
Sheen (Hawkman)#1667 or lessAccepting him costs 10
Debonair (General)#2534 or moreAisha and Saradin in your army; Magnus’s squad takes Ibu Deli
Destin (Lord)#2934 or moreAisha, Saradin, and Debonair in your army; Magnus’s squad goes to Kurashino. Turning him down costs 5
Gilbert (Beast Master)#2968 or moreJoins with Destin when you accept Destin’s offer; from 34 to 67 Destin comes alone
Carth (Black Knight)#33No checkCarth survives the mission, and Aisha, Saradin, Debonair, Destin, and Gilbert haven’t joined. Accepting him adds 10; refusing costs 10

Ending. The final scenes check your Chaos Frame band: low (0–33), middle (34–67), or high (68–100). Each band leads to a different ending, and the low ending has two versions depending on who is in your army.

  • Promises (#38). Above 33, Frederick sends Magnus off with his blessing; at 33 or below he warns Magnus that he has grown too fond of war.
  • Flaum the Archangel. During the Area Investigation of March on the Capital (#37), Flaum gives Magnus a gift if Chaos Frame is 50 or more, several earlier story events have happened, and you visit at the right time of day; otherwise he scolds him as “narrow-minded”.
  • Townspeople. In a few Area Investigation towns, what the locals say to you depends on your Chaos Frame.

Goth. Every completed scenario pays a population bonus that grows the further Chaos Frame is from 50, in either direction, and twice as fast below 50; see Scenario rewards.

Worked example

A squad of a Knight (Alignment 60), a Fighter (55), and a Cleric (65) averages 60. At a town with Morale 50 the difference is 10, so the score is 10–17: “liberated” with +1, or 0 if the roll is high. The same squad at a town with Morale 20 scores 40–47: “captured” and −1. Swapping in a Chaotic Ninja (Alignment 25) for the Cleric brings the average to 46, and the Morale-20 town now scores 26–33, usually a liberation.

Tips

  • Send a matching squad. Check a town’s Morale before you take it, and send the squad whose average Alignment is closest.
  • Defend what you liberate. Every stronghold an enemy retakes costs 2, and taking it back may cost more.
  • Mind the † towns. Taking them lowers Chaos Frame whoever does it, so leave them unless you need them.
  • Know your targets. Liedel, Debonair, Destin, and Gilbert want a high Chaos Frame; Sheen won’t come at 68 or more. Decide early which recruits and which ending you want.
  • Weigh story answers. Recruiting Sheen lowers Chaos Frame, while recruiting Vad, Biske, or Carth raises it. Europea costs 5 when she joins but earns 20 later if she is still with you.
  • A low Chaos Frame pays more Goth. The population bonus below 50 is twice as large as above it.
  • Plan for Alignment first. A squad’s average moves as its members fight; see Alignment.

Chaos Frame glossary

Chaos Frame

Your army’s hidden reputation with the people, from 0 to 100. It starts at 50 and decides some recruits, the ending, and part of each scenario’s Goth reward.

Town Morale

A stronghold’s leaning, from 0 to 100. A squad whose average Alignment is close to it liberates the town; a squad far from it captures the town.

Town penalty

A hidden 40 points added to the score of a few strongholds, so taking them always lowers Chaos Frame.

Chaos Frame band

The third your Chaos Frame falls in: low (0–33), middle (34–67), or high (68–100). The ending and some story scenes check only the band.

Modder reference: Chaos Frame

Chaos Frame is one saved byte. Its writers are the new-game initialisers, the stronghold takeover formula, the enemy-retake rule, and 39 stores in the event scripts (director command 0xB6 exists but no retail Director stream uses it). Its readers are the event scripts (recruitment gates, ending flags, scene variants), director query 0xBE, the scenario Goth settlement, and the staff-roll display.

Where these facts come from

Locations were read from the US retail ROM (z64); the stronghold code runs in the scenario overlay at z64 + 0x800AB8C0 and the director parser in its own overlay. Recruitment thresholds, the Scene 4/5 order change, and the ending descriptions come from the wiki mission pages. None of the suggested edits has been tried in a running game yet, so test each one from a cold boot before relying on it.

The takeover and retake code is outside the CRC-checked region; the new-game value is inside it.

What do you want to change?

Make liberation kinder or harsher

Change the band thresholds or deltas in the takeover formula.

See Stronghold takeover

Stop a town from moving Chaos Frame

Set its ktenmain Morale byte to 0xFF.

See Stronghold takeover · Enemy retake

Add a scripted Chaos Frame change

Insert a director 0xB6 command with a signed-byte delta.

See Scripted changes and queries

How to read the code and byte evidence

ROM offsets use big-endian z64 order. The master v64 stores each byte pair in reverse order. RAM addresses belong to the stated overlay or structure.

Each code line shows the z64 offset, the four original bytes, and the MIPS instruction. Relative branches name z64 destinations; J/JAL targets are encoded RAM addresses. The instruction after a branch is its delay slot.

Samples are stored bytes, not calculated values. For compressed resources, the sample gives the container’s ROM offset and the offset inside the decoded file.

Chaos Frame fieldStronghold takeoverEnemy retakeScripted changes and queriesOther consumers

Chaos Frame field

One byte. The takeover, retake, and 0xB6 paths clamp it to 0–100; the event interpreter’s set-variable path (opcodes 0x70–0x77, variable 0xFF, store at 0x00047360) stores the script’s value without a clamp. The save codec keeps seven bits.

Neighbours
0x801936A7 is the runtime scenario key; 0x801936AA is set to 7 by the same initialisers.
Flag overlap
Persistent flag IDs 280–287 would address the Chaos Frame byte’s bits; no retail use is known.

Stronghold takeover

Member Alignment comes from each valid member (IDs 1–98) of the five-slot unit; an empty unit counts as 50. The score is a u16, so penalty and random terms stack on the absolute difference.

Bands
0–5 +2, 6–15 +1, 16–30 0, 31–50 −1, 51–80 −2, 81–110 −3, 111–140 −4, 141+ −5.
Message
func_0010DDB4 (0x0010EB4C–0x0010EB84) picks the “liberated” family (base 0x10) only for an enemy-held site (+0x1C bit 0x0004) and switches to “captured” (0x29) when the takeover returns 1; every other site uses the “captured” family. The other callers ignore the return value.
Census
Of 316 ktenmain records, 48 have Morale 0xFF and 9 have bit 7 set. Most, but not all, enemy headquarters are 0xFF (Fort Bergiga, Fort Romulus, and Castle Andvari have ordinary Morale); Dardunnelles and Castle Echel are 0xFF without being headquarters.
Morale source
Site +0x1E equals the ktenmain byte at runtime; no code writes 0x801951CE. The wiki differs for Kaezi, Lachook, and Coongul.

Enemy retake

An enemy unit heading for a site (+0x7C) that reaches it with no player unit in range flips the site and costs 2, unless the site is 0xFF.

Flags
Site +0x1C: 0x0002 player-held, 0x0004 enemy-held.
Trigger
The enemy unit’s +0x78 bit 0x10000, set at 0x00109F10 only when its target site is player-held and not enemy-held.

Scripted changes and queries

The resident event interpreter (func_00046854) runs [opcode, operand] pairs from the 115-row event directory (resource key 0x003A5668, custom-LZ). Chaos Frame is property 0xFF: 60–67 FF loads it, 70–77 FF stores it. Every retail store is 60ff 69NN d102 9019 0101 6800 70ff (max(CF − NN, 0)) or 60ff 69NN 9011 6964 c101 0101 6864 70ff (min(CF + NN, 100)).

Encoding
68–6F nn immediate, 88–8F nn high byte, 90–97 ALU (operand bits 3+ select and/or/add/sub, bits 0–2 the source), A1–FF compare-and-branch (target = next word + s8 operand), 01 nn relative jump, 10 00 launch Director selector r0, 15 nn history record. Variables below 0xE4 dispatch through getter table z64 0x000650B0 and setter table 0x00065120 (high five bits select, low three bits pick the index register): 60 61 = flag[r1], 71 60 sets flag[r0] = r1, 6x 9x reads dialogue-control byte 0x8019EE40+index.
Choices
Two-answer dialogue lines write slot 3 with serifu @w3001 (answer 1) or @w3255 (answer 2); scripts test 63 91 against 255.
Counts
39 stores in 29 labelled events; 45 reads (recruit gates, ending flags 162/163 in row 114, scene variants). Mylesia’s −10 (row 7) is skipped when flag 0x6A is set, which the Zenobian Border row (row 8) does.
Rows
Rows 4–64 each set the runtime key (property 0xE9) of the mission they start; rows 71–109 repeat the keys for Area Investigation.

CHARACTER & CAMPAIGN

Shops

Where every shop is, what each one sells, and what everything costs.

Shops are in some of the towns on most mission maps. Every shop sells the same seven expendables, plus its own fixed selection of equipment. To shop, send a squad to the town and use the town’s shop from there.

How shops work

  • Every shop has the same expendables. Heal Leaf, Heal Seed, Heal Pack, Power Fruit, Angel Fruit, Revive Stone, and Quit Gate are on sale everywhere.
  • Equipment varies by shop. Each shop has a fixed list, and towns in different missions sometimes share one.
  • Prices are the same everywhere. Each item has one price in every shop that sells it. The one exception is the Annihilation spellbook, whose price rises as the campaign goes on.
  • A few items have their own shop. Altar of Resurrection and some quest items are sold only by a special shopkeeper in Melphy on certain days. Rare treasures come from drops, rewards, and events.

Annihilation costs 30,000 Goth at the start of the campaign and 20 Goth more for every day that passes, up to 60,000. By the time you reach Vertze, the only shop that sells it, the price is far above 30,000.

Check a class’s slot types before buying; a slot only takes items of one exact type. See How equipment works.

Melphy’s special shop

Melphy, in Dardunnelles (missions #8 and #19), has no ordinary shop. Instead, a shopkeeper there sells rare items on set days of each month. Enter the Melphy stronghold on the right day and at the right time to buy them. Most squads need to set out the day before to arrive in time.

Altar of Resurrection can’t be bought anywhere else, though several are hidden on mission maps. Bolt of Silk and Condrite are needed for the Princess and Dragoon classes; see Changing class.

Tips

  • Stock up on Heal Pack early. It is available in every shop and heals every standing member of a squad.
  • Buy one of each class’s gear. Owning a single copy lets class changes buy further copies automatically; see Changing class.
  • Check for better stock ahead. Later missions often sell stronger versions of the same types, so a big purchase can wait for the next shop.
  • Watch your Goth. Mission rewards are your main income; see Scenario rewards.

Shop glossary

Shop stock

The equipment a shop sells. It is fixed for each shop, and several towns can share the same stock.

Expendables

The seven everyday items every shop sells: Heal Leaf, Heal Seed, Heal Pack, Power Fruit, Angel Fruit, Revive Stone, and Quit Gate.

Modder reference: Shops

A shop is a site with a ktenmain shop index. Opening it builds one combined list (seven fixed expendables, then the shop’s equipment) and splits it into two arrays. The Editor’s Shops tab replaces the list per shop through a runtime hook.

Where these facts come from

Locations were read from the US retail ROM (z64). The per-town stock was parsed from archives #751 and #691 with the Editor’s parsers; 34 of 35 shops appear on the wiki storefront lists and all 34 match. The Melphy special-shop days come from the wiki only. None of the suggested edits has been tried in a running game yet, so test each one from a cold boot before relying on it.

Where the data lives

Shop edits go through the Editor’s runtime override (50 equipment and 15 consumables per shop at most), not by rewriting archive #751.

What do you want to change?

Change what a shop sells

Use the Editor’s Shops tab; it writes a per-shop override list.

See Shop list producer · List split

Give a town a shop

Set its ktenmain B27 index. The producer reads only B27; B25 bit 0 is set on every shop record in retail, but no reader of it was found.

See Shop data · Shop site

How to read the code and byte evidence

ROM offsets use big-endian z64 order. The master v64 stores each byte pair in reverse order. RAM addresses belong to the stated overlay or structure.

Each code line shows the z64 offset, the four original bytes, and the MIPS instruction. Relative branches name z64 destinations; J/JAL targets are encoded RAM addresses. The instruction after a branch is its delay slot.

Samples are stored bytes, not calculated values. For compressed resources, the sample gives the container’s ROM offset and the offset inside the decoded file.

Shop list producer

The producer writes the seven literal consumable IDs for every shop, so the Expendables tab is identical everywhere; Altar of Resurrection (ID 7) is absent and is sold only by Melphy’s special shopkeeper.

List split

Bit-15 entries go to the equipment array with the bit cleared; plain entries go to the consumable array. The fill has no bounds checks, so 50 and 15 are overflow ceilings, not tested maxima.

Shop data

35 shops. 45 ktenmain records carry a shop index, but five are never used as a mission site: the objectives Tacikent (#10) and Dardunnelles (#301) and group-1 records #0 Shafsabus, #6 Gerall Avad, and #9 Tobolisk. The remaining 40 records cover 38 town names. Shop 31’s only record, #280 Tobolisk, is reached only through runtime key 63, which has no confident mission match.

Wiki differences
Every documented list matches. The wiki spells Glamdring “Glamdring (aka Slamdring)”, prices Takua’s Hard Leather at 50 (150 in the ROM and every other shop), and lists Apertine for Scene 43, which the key 59 sites don’t include.
Objective records
Neither the producer nor the command handler reads B24; the objective records simply aren’t sites.

CHARACTER & CAMPAIGN

Scenario rewards

How much Goth and how many Soldiers you get for finishing a scenario.

Completing a scenario pays out Goth and adds Soldiers to your reserves. Both rewards depend on the strongholds you hold when the scenario ends. The Goth reward also depends on your Chaos Frame, and the Soldier count on each town’s Morale.

What counts

Both rewards count the strongholds in the current scenario that are yours when it ends. What matters is who holds each stronghold at that moment, not which ones you visited along the way. If completing the scenario captures a final stronghold, the game marks it as yours before paying out, so it counts too.

RewardDepends onNot affected by
GothThe scenario’s base amount, the total population of your strongholds, and Chaos FrameTown Morale, character Alignment, random chance
SoldiersEach stronghold’s population and Morale, and the room left in your reservesChaos Frame, character Alignment, random chance

Scripted items and story rewards are separate and aren’t covered here.

Goth

Every scenario pays a fixed amount of base Goth. On top of that you get a population bonus, which grows the further your Chaos Frame is from 50 in either direction.

Chaos Frame below 50: bonus = (50 − Chaos Frame) × population ÷ 25
Chaos Frame 50 or more: bonus = (Chaos Frame − 50) × population ÷ 50
 
Goth reward = base Goth + bonus, with the bonus rounded down

Here, population is the combined population of all your strongholds in the scenario. The two divisors differ, so a low Chaos Frame pays twice the bonus of an equally high one. At exactly 50 the bonus is zero and you get only the base amount.

Example: base Goth 5,000 and total population 1,000

Chaos FramePopulation bonusGoth reward
050 × 1,000 ÷ 25 = 2,0007,000
4010 × 1,000 ÷ 25 = 4005,400
5005,000
6010 × 1,000 ÷ 50 = 2005,200
10050 × 1,000 ÷ 50 = 1,0006,000

The bonus is rounded down before it is added. Chaos Frame 60 with a population of 999 gives a bonus of 199.8, which becomes 199.

Some base amounts

ScenarioBase Goth
Tenne Plains500
Volmus Mine I600
Volmus Mine II1,500
Alba2,250

You can’t hold more than 9,999,999 Goth, so anything above that is lost. Chaos Frame affects the payout, but the payout doesn’t change Chaos Frame.

Soldiers

Each of your strongholds contributes Soldiers on its own, based on its population and its town Morale.

Soldiers from one stronghold = population × Morale ÷ 10,000
rounded down, with a minimum of 1

Every stronghold you hold gives at least one Soldier, however small it is. A stronghold with no Morale value counts as Morale 50.

Example: three strongholds

StrongholdPopulationMoraleSoldiers
A50060500 × 60 ÷ 10,000 = 3
B30040300 × 40 ÷ 10,000 = 1.2, rounded down to 1
C5000, raised to the minimum of 1
Total5

Each stronghold is rounded separately before the results are added, so several small towns can give more Soldiers than one big town with the same total population.

Soldier Reserves hold at most 200, and any Soldiers beyond that are lost. In the example, if you already had 198 in reserve, only two of the five would be added.

Related rules

Capturing strongholds changes Chaos Frame during the scenario, depending on how well each squad’s Alignment suits the town. See Alignment and strongholds.

After the rewards, the game checks whether fallen characters become Angel Knights or Zombies. See Automatic class changes.

Reward glossary

Population

The number of people living in a stronghold. Your strongholds’ populations are added together for the Goth bonus, and each one sets that stronghold’s Soldier contribution.

Town Morale

A stronghold’s own Morale. It decides how many Soldiers that town contributes, but it has no effect on the Goth reward.

Chaos Frame

Your army’s hidden reputation, from 0 to 100. The further it is from 50, the bigger the Goth population bonus. It is separate from character Alignment and from town Morale.

Base Goth

The fixed amount of Goth a scenario pays before the population bonus is added.

Modder reference: Scenario Rewards

Scenario rewards come from three stored inputs and one piece of code. The inputs are each scenario’s base Goth, each stronghold’s population and Morale, and your Chaos Frame. The code is a settlement routine that adds the bonus and applies the caps. The base Goth table is a plain ROM table. Population and Morale live in a compressed archive that the Editor already edits.

Where these facts come from

Every location and value on this tab was read from the US retail ROM, and offsets are z64. None of the suggested edits has been tried in a running game yet, so test each one from a cold boot before relying on it.

Where the data lives

DataLocationFormatIn the Editor
Base Gothz64 0x0013C55A + 12 × scenario keyu16, big-endianNot exposed
Stronghold populationktenmain.bin record +22 (LH5 archive at z64 0x027451AE)u16Scenario tab, site Population
Stronghold Moralektenmain.bin record +24Low 7 bits; FF means none and counts as 50Scenario tab, site Morale
Chaos FrameRAM 0x801936A9u8, 0–100Save Game Editor
GothRAM 0x80196A6Cu32, capped at 9,999,999Save Game Editor
Soldier ReservesRAM 0x80190F80u8, capped at 200Not exposed

None of the reward data sits inside the CRC-checked region (z64 0x1000–0x100FFF).

The exact arithmetic

StepRule
Goth bonus(50 − C) × P ÷ 25 when C < 50, otherwise (C − 50) × P ÷ 50. It uses signed 32-bit arithmetic and truncates toward zero.
Goth paidmin(9,999,999, Goth + base + bonus), compared unsigned
Soldiers per strongholdt = f32(P × f32(M ÷ 100)), then max(1, trunc(t × 0.01)) with the last multiply in double precision
Soldier totalThe sum over captured strongholds, keeping only the low byte
Soldiers paidmin(total, 200 − reserves)

C is Chaos Frame, P is population, and M is effective Morale. Scenario key 54 calculates both rewards but pays neither.

What do you want to change?

Change a scenario’s base Goth

Change how many Soldiers a town gives

Work out why a reward came out smaller than expected

Check which strongholds were flagged as yours, then the one-byte Soldier wrap, then the caps.

See Which strongholds count · Soldier award per stronghold · Settlement: Goth bonus and caps

Trace when rewards are paid

The scenario update calls settlement, and settlement pays only if its completion check passes.

See Where settlement is called · Completion check · Settlement: Goth bonus and caps

How to read the code and byte evidence

ROM offsets use big-endian z64 order. The master v64 stores each byte pair in reverse order. RAM addresses belong to the stated overlay or structure.

Each code line shows the z64 offset, the four original bytes, and the MIPS instruction. Relative branches name z64 destinations; J/JAL targets are encoded RAM addresses. The instruction after a branch is its delay slot.

Samples are stored bytes, not calculated values. For compressed resources, the sample gives the container’s ROM offset and the offset inside the decoded file.

Base Goth tableStronghold population and MoraleSettlement: Goth bonus and capsWhich strongholds countSoldier award per strongholdCompletion checkWhere settlement is called

Base Goth table

Each scenario key has a 12-byte record in a 65-record table, and the last two bytes are its base Goth. The key is the staged scenario key the game uses internally, which isn’t the same as the wiki’s scenario numbering.

Location
Record at z64 0x0013C550 + 12 × key; base Goth at 0x0013C55A + 12 × key (u16, big-endian).
Keys
0–64. Key 0 is the world map. Key 1 is Tenne Plains, 2 is Volmus Mine I, 6 is Volmus Mine II, and 9 is Alba. Keys 44–64 include alternate and internal entries.
Example
Tenne Plains (key 1) at 0x0013C55C: 00 01 00 04 02 08 05 11 04 00 01 F4. The last two bytes, 01 F4, are 500.
Other fields
Byte +5 selects the scenario’s stronghold list (SCINCSV). The other bytes aren’t mapped here.
Current key
RAM 0x8018F481 (u8).
In the Editor
Not exposed.

How to change it

Write a new big-endian value to the last two bytes of the record. For example, 03 E8 at 0x0013C566 makes Tenne Plains pay 1,000 base Goth. The table is outside the CRC region.

Watch out for

  • Key 54 is an internal entry. It stores 7,120 Goth, but settlement skips its payout entirely.
  • A base of 0 doesn’t remove the population bonus. Keys 10, 22, 35, and 62 store 0.
  • Don’t match keys to wiki scenario numbers by position. Read the key the game stages at 0x8018F481.

Stronghold population and Morale

Each stronghold’s static data is a 28-byte record in ktenmain.bin, stored LH5-compressed in an LHA archive. Scenarios choose their strongholds from this list by one-based record ID. At scenario load the values are copied into 36-byte live records, and the reward code reads those.

Location
LHA archive at z64 0x027451AE (LH5, 8,848 bytes decoded, 316 records). Record N starts at decoded offset 28 × (N − 1).
Fields
+1–+20 name · +22 population (u16) · +24 Morale in the low 7 bits (FF = none) · +25 capability mask · +26 type · +27 shop index
Example
Record 1, Shafsabus: population 02 C0 = 704, Morale 59 = 89.
Live records
RAM 0x801951B0 + 36 × site index: +0x1C flags, +0x1E Morale byte, +0x20 population. The live count is at 0x801F1070.
In the Editor
Scenario tab: each site’s Population and Morale. The Editor recompresses the archive on export.

How to change it

Use the Editor’s Scenario tab. A hand edit has to decompress ktenmain.bin, change the record, recompress it, and repack the archive. Decoded offsets are not ROM offsets.

Watch out for

  • Several scenarios can use the same record, so a change applies everywhere that stronghold appears.
  • FF in +24 also marks mission objectives.
  • Bit 7 of +24 adds a 40-point penalty when a squad liberates the town (see the Alignment reference). The Soldier award ignores it, and the Editor keeps it unchanged.

Settlement: Goth bonus and caps

func_001390F0 pays both rewards. It adds base Goth to the population bonus and clamps the wallet at 9,999,999. It then adds Soldiers up to the reserve cap of 200. The division by 25 or 50 uses a multiply by reciprocal (0x51EB851F) that truncates toward zero.

Code
func_001390F0 (z64 0x001390F0–0x00139C10), running at RAM 0x801E49B0.
Inputs
Staged key 0x8018F481 · Chaos Frame 0x801936A9 (u8) · population total from Which strongholds count
Outputs
Goth 0x80196A6C (u32) · Soldier Reserves 0x80190F80 (u8). Admitted Soldiers are also added to the character count at 0x80190F81.
Intermediate
Calculated Goth at 0x8021C744; calculated Soldiers at 0x8021C748.
Caps
The wallet is compared unsigned against 0x0098967F (9,999,999); reserves stop at 200.
Special key
Key 54 calculates both rewards but pays neither.

How to change it

The divisors and both caps are constants in this function. The reserve count is one byte, so a reserve cap above 255 can’t work without widening that field.

Watch out for

  • Custom values use 32-bit arithmetic, so very large populations or base amounts overflow instead of behaving like ordinary numbers.
  • The Soldier total has already been cut to one byte by Soldier award per stronghold before the reserve cap applies.

Which strongholds count

This helper loops over the live site records and adds up the population of every row whose flags contain 0x0002, meaning the site is yours. Flag 0x0004 on its own doesn’t count. The Soldier helper uses the same test.

Code
func_00127BFC (z64 0x00127BFC–0x00127C50), running at RAM 0x801D34BC.
Records
Live rows at RAM 0x801951B0, 36 bytes each; loop count at 0x801F1070.
Fields
+0x1C flags (u16) · +0x20 population (u16)
Capture
func_0010DDB4 clears 0x0004 and sets 0x0002 when you take a site. Settlement does the same for the final site at z64 0x001398B4–0x001398D8.

How to change it

To test rewards, set or clear 0x0002 in a live row’s flags before settlement runs.

Watch out for

  • The helper’s own base pointer, 0x801951CC, points at +0x1C of the first row. Don’t mix its offsets with full-row offsets.
  • Static ktenmain records are 28 bytes, but live records are 36.

Soldier award per stronghold

For each captured row, this helper first reads the Morale byte: FF becomes 50, and any other value keeps its low 7 bits. It then computes population × Morale ÷ 100 in single precision, multiplies by 0.01 in double precision, and truncates, using 1 whenever the result is 0. It adds up the contributions and returns only the low byte, so a total of 256 becomes 0.

Code
func_00127C50 (z64 0x00127C50–0x00127D30), running at RAM 0x801D3510.
Coefficient
0.01 as a double. Matching bytes exist at z64 0x00142F30, but whether the code loads them from there isn’t confirmed.
Return
The low byte of the summed contributions.

How to change it

The simplest way to raise Soldier awards is to raise a stronghold’s population or Morale in the Scenario tab. To change the 0.01 coefficient, first confirm where the running code loads it from.

Watch out for

  • Because of the one-byte wrap, large modded populations can shrink the award. A total of 260 pays 4.
  • Keep the single-then-double precision order if you reimplement the formula.

Completion check

Settlement pays out only when its completion check passes. The ordinary check tests flag 0x10 on a selected map unit, with special cases for keys 8, 45, and 46. What that flag means in play hasn’t been pinned down.

Code
func_00139C10 (z64 0x00139C10–0x00139C88).

Watch out for

  • Don’t assume the flag means “all enemies defeated” or “boss killed”. Neither has been shown.

Where settlement is called

The scenario update calls settlement on its normal path every time it runs, so reaching that call doesn’t mean rewards are paid. Settlement makes its own completion check first.

Code
func_00102FA0 (z64 0x00102FA0–0x00104D74); the call is in 0x00103AF0–0x00103B0C.
Next state
After settlement, the event state at RAM 0x801F0DE0 becomes 0x1B.

Watch out for

  • Use this call as a breakpoint target, not as proof of a payout.
